sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.summary: Introduces Chapter 3 on Earthwork, Hydraulic, and Underwater Fills. Covers scope of the chapter including compaction theory, engineering behavior of fill materials, construction and control guidelines, compaction requirements, embankment design, and hydraulic/underwater fill construction. Also defines earthwork as a manufacturing process and explains the purpose of compaction.
key_points: Chapter covers design and construction of compacted earth, hydraulic fill, and underwater fill.
Topics include compaction theory, engineering behavior of fill materials, construction control, and embankment design.
Earthwork is defined as the process of changing topography to accommodate construction and provide drainage.
Earthwork is a manufacturing process using soil or rock: excavation, transport, placement, and amendment.
Compaction is the final step in the earthwork process — removal of air from soil via temporary mechanical load (rolling, tamping, or vibration).
sections.applicability: Applies whenever earthwork, compacted fill, hydraulic fill, or underwater fill design and construction is being performed.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: Defines the scope of Chapter 3, which covers compacted earth, hydraulic, and underwater fill design and construction. Includes compaction theory, fill material behavior, construction process guidelines, compaction requirements for various applications and equipment, embankment design requirements, and hydraulic fill construction on land and underwater.
sections.body: This chapter summarizes the design and construction of compacted earth, hydraulic fill, and underwater fill. It explains the theory of compaction and the engineering behavior of fill materials. Guidelines for the construction process and control of compacted fills are provided, along with compaction requirements for various applications and equipment. General requirements for the design of various types of embankments are included. The construction and control of hydraulic fills, both on land and underwater, are discussed.
key_points: Covers design and construction of compacted earth, hydraulic fill, and underwater fill.
Explains compaction theory and engineering behavior of fill materials.
Provides construction process guidelines and compaction control requirements.
Addresses compaction requirements for various applications and equipment types.
Includes embankment design requirements and hydraulic fill construction on land and underwater.
sections.applicability: Applies to any project involving compacted earth fills, hydraulic fills, or underwater fills requiring design and construction guidance.

sections.title: Earthwork Process and Purpose of Compaction
sections.summary: Defines earthwork as a manufacturing process using soil or rock that changes topography for construction and drainage. Describes the four stages — excavation, transport, placement, and amendment — with compaction as the final step. Compaction removes air from soil through temporary mechanical loading such as rolling, tamping, or vibration, as illustrated in Figure 3-1.
sections.body: Earthwork is the process of changing the topography to accommodate construction and to provide drainage. As illustrated in Figure 3-1, earthwork is a manufacturing process using soil or rock, and includes excavation, transport, placement, and amendment. The final step of the process is compaction, which refers to the removal of air from the soil by the temporary application of a mechanical load, such as rolling, tamping, or vibration.
key_points: Earthwork changes topography to accommodate construction and provide drainage.
Earthwork is a manufacturing process involving four steps: excavation, transport, placement, and amendment.
Compaction is the final step: removal of air from soil by temporary mechanical loading.
Mechanical loading methods include rolling, tamping, and vibration.
Figure 3-1 illustrates earthwork objectives and methodology.
sections.applicability: Applies when understanding the fundamental definition and purpose of compaction within the broader earthwork construction process.

sections.title: COMPACTION THEORY
sections.summary: Overview of compaction theory covering weight-volume relationships, graphical representations, characterization methods for soils with and without fines, and the effect of compaction on engineering properties including strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity.
sections.body: This section summarizes the weight volume relationships involved in the process of compaction and how those relationships are represented graphically. Methods for characterizing the level of compaction are discussed for soils both with and without appreciable amounts of fines. Finally, this section explores the effect of compaction on the engineering properties of soil.
key_points: Compaction theory addresses weight-volume relationships and their graphical representation on the compaction plane.
Characterization differs for soils with appreciable fines (relative compaction, R.C.) vs. coarse-grained soils with little fines (relative density, Dr).
Compaction affects strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity — three key objectives of controlled fill construction.
The section covers both coarse-grained and fine-grained soil behavior under compaction.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever compaction theory must be understood for design, specification, or quality control of controlled compacted fill.

sections.title: Process of Compaction
sections.summary: Defines dry unit weight and degree of saturation as the fundamental weight-volume parameters governing compaction. Explains how compaction removes air voids, illustrated with phase diagrams at different points on the compaction plane, and why further compaction beyond certain states requires water removal.
sections.body:
Compaction focuses on changing the dry unit weight (γd) of soil (and rock) which is defined as:

(Ws / Vt) = γt / (1 + w/100)   (3-1)

where: Ws = weight of solids, Vt = total volume, γt = total unit weight, and w = water content (percentage).

The degree of saturation (S), which is the percentage of the void space filled with water, is also important to understanding the behavior and construction of controlled fill. The dry unit weight is related to S by:

γd = (S · γw) / (S · w/100 + Gs · w/100) ... [Eq. 3-2]

where: γw = unit weight of water = 62.4 pcf, w = water content (percentage), and Gs = specific gravity of solids.

To illustrate the compaction process, phase diagrams are shown in Figure 3-2 for different points on the compaction plane, which plots dry unit weight against water content. Moving from left to right on the compaction plane (A→C→E), the dry unit weight stays constant but the amount of water in the voids increases with the water content. In other words, the degree of saturation (S) increases. In order to compact the soil, a compactive effort must be applied to the soil to remove void space in the form of air, following paths similar to A→B or C→D. Further compaction of the soil at Points D or E is not possible unless water is removed, and the water content is decreased.
key_points: Dry unit weight (γd) is defined as the weight of solids divided by total volume, or equivalently total unit weight divided by (1 + w/100).
Degree of saturation (S) is the percentage of void space filled with water; it increases as water content increases at constant dry unit weight.
Compaction removes air voids; once air can no longer escape (high S), further compaction requires reducing water content.
Phase diagrams on the compaction plane (γd vs. w) visualize the transitions during compaction and wetting.

equations.description: Dry unit weight definition: γd = Ws/Vt = γt / (1 + w/100), where Ws = weight of solids, Vt = total volume, γt = total unit weight, w = water content (%).
Dry unit weight as a function of degree of saturation: γd = (S·γw) / (S·w/100 + Gs·w/100... full form relates γd to S, γw, w, and Gs; γw = 62.4 pcf.

sections.applicability: Applies when establishing fundamental weight-volume relationships for any soil or rock being evaluated for compaction.

sections.title: Characterizing Compaction
sections.summary: Container section covering methods for characterizing the level of compaction in soils. Distinguishes between soils with appreciable fines (using compaction curves, relative compaction, and relative water content) and coarse-grained soils with little fines (using relative density and void ratio extremes).
key_points: Compaction characterization methods differ based on fines content (threshold approximately 5–15% passing #200 sieve).
For soils with fines: relative compaction (R.C.) and relative water content (Δw) compared to a standard Proctor compaction curve.
For soils with little fines: relative density (Dr) using emax and emin from ASTM D4254 and D4253.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the appropriate compaction characterization method based on soil fines content.

sections.title: Soils with Appreciable Fines
sections.summary: Describes compaction curve theory for soils with >5–15% fines, explaining maximum dry unit weight and optimum water content. Covers standard and modified Proctor energy levels, the line of optimums, dry vs. wet of optimum states, relative compaction (R.C.), and relative water content (Δw). Notes special cases where field conditions differ from laboratory results.
sections.body:
For soils with more than about 5% to 15% fines (i.e., particles passing the #200 sieve), compacted soil behavior is often idealized using the concave-down compaction curves shown in Figure 3-3. These curves were first explained by Proctor (1933) in an effort to improve the quality of fill for earth dam construction. A compaction curve is obtained when soil is compacted using a constant compactive effort, which is the amount of work performed on the soil per unit volume during compaction. Hogentogler (1936) further explained compaction in terms of lubrication and particle hydration and noted that air becomes trapped at water contents higher than optimum. Barden and Sides (1970) later confirmed that the peak in the compaction curve occurs at the degree of saturation where air is no longer able to flow freely from the soil during compaction. The compaction process has also been explained in terms of the effective stresses that develop during compaction (Olson 1963) and capillary pressures in the unsaturated state (Hilf 1956).

All of these theories provide valuable insight into the behavior of compacted soil. As the water content increases, less compactive effort is required to break up the lumps of soil. However, once air can no longer easily leave the soil, additional water simply takes up space and prevents higher levels of compaction. This creates a peak in the compaction curve. The dry unit weight at the peak of a particular compaction curve is referred to as the maximum dry unit weight (γd,max) for the corresponding compactive effort. The water content corresponding to the peak of a compaction curve is called the optimum water content (wopt). If the compaction energy is increased, the compaction curve shifts toward lower water contents and higher dry unit weights. The relationship between the change in compactive effort and the shift of compaction curve is highly nonlinear.

The two most common levels of compactive effort are standard Proctor (ASTM D698) and modified Proctor (ASTM D1557). Standard Proctor is more often used as the reference energy for compaction control. The compactive effort for standard Proctor is 12,400 lbf-ft/ft3. Modified Proctor was originally developed for compaction of airfield pavement subgrades. The compactive effort for modified Proctor is 56,000 lbf-ft/ft3. Modified Proctor is sometimes used as the reference standard for compaction of the upper few feet of a heavily loaded fill.

The peaks of a series of compaction curves can be connected to form a line of optimums, which often corresponds to S in the range of 75 to 85%. Compaction to a state to the left of this curve is referred to as dry of optimum while compaction states to the right are termed wet of optimum. All possible compaction states for a particular soil are bounded on the right side by the S = 100% curve (a.k.a., zero air voids curve). Properties typically associated with "dry" and "wet" compaction are summarized in Figure 3-3.

The dry unit weight and water content of a compacted soil can be compared to the conditions at the peak of a compaction curve for the same soil. Relative compaction (R.C.) is used for soils with appreciable fines and is defined as:

R.C. = (γd,field / γd,max) × 100%   (3-3)

where: γd,field = dry unit weight of compacted fill and γd,max = maximum dry unit weight for a specified compactive effort.

The relative water content (Δw) of the compacted fill is:

Δw = wfield − wopt   (3-4)

where: wfield = water content of the compacted fill.

The position and shape of the compaction curve can be affected by variables other than compactive effort. For example, different methods of applying the compactive effort, such as kneading compaction, impact compaction, and static compaction, result in different soil structure and change the compaction curves. Similarly, different types of field compaction equipment result in different compaction behavior.

Some soils and rocks undergo irreversible changes during drying and compaction, and they may exhibit drastically different compaction curves in the field compared to those created in the laboratory unless special care is taken. These materials include clays containing halloysite or allophane minerals, which are chemically altered when dried (Hilf 1991). Some weak rocks may degrade differently during field and laboratory compaction. Very dense glacial till clays can have field compacted dry unit weights much higher than the laboratory γd,max because of the extensive loosening required to perform the laboratory compaction tests.
key_points: Compaction curves (γd vs. w) exhibit a peak at γd,max and wopt; peak occurs where air can no longer flow freely from soil during compaction.
Standard Proctor (ASTM D698): 12,400 lbf-ft/ft³; Modified Proctor (ASTM D1557): 56,000 lbf-ft/ft³. Higher energy shifts curve to lower w and higher γd.
Line of optimums typically corresponds to S = 75–85%; the S = 100% (zero air voids) curve bounds all possible compaction states on the right.
Relative compaction R.C. = (γd,field / γd,max) × 100%; relative water content Δw = wfield − wopt.
Some materials (halloysite/allophane clays, weak rocks, dense glacial tills) may show significantly different field vs. laboratory compaction behavior.
Compaction method (kneading, impact, static) and equipment type affect the shape and position of the compaction curve.

equations.description: Relative compaction: R.C. = (γd,field / γd,max) × 100%, where γd,field = dry unit weight of compacted fill and γd,max = maximum dry unit weight for a specified compactive effort.
Relative water content: Δw = wfield − wopt, where wfield = water content of compacted fill and wopt = optimum water content.

sections.applicability: Applies to soils with more than approximately 5–15% fines (passing #200 sieve) where compaction curve behavior is well-defined.

sections.title: Compaction of Soils with Little Fines
sections.summary: Covers characterization of compaction for coarse-grained soils with less than ~5–15% fines, where compaction curves are poorly defined. Introduces maximum and minimum void ratios (emax, emin) from ASTM D4254 and D4253, and defines relative density (Dr) using both void ratio and dry unit weight formulations as the primary compaction metric.
sections.body:
For soils without an appreciable fines content (i.e., F < 5 to 15%), compaction behavior is much less sensitive to water content. In some cases, the compaction curve is poorly defined below optimum (Sowers 1979). In other soils, a minimum value of γd may be reached at a midrange water content because the bulking of sand or gravel grains inhibits compaction (Hilf 1991).

For these materials, characterization in terms of void ratio can be more appropriate. The loosest state that the soil can sustain with a regular structure is referred to as the maximum void ratio (emax) and can be found using ASTM D4254. The densest configuration of the soil is called the minimum void ratio (emin) and can be found using a vibratory table as described in ASTM D4253. The value of emin depends on particle shape and size. Some compaction methods and levels of compactive effort may break particles, which can lower emin (Sowers 1979). Corresponding values of minimum dry unit weight (γd,min) and maximum dry unit weight (γd,max) can be calculated. The value of emin determined by ASTM D4253 corresponds to approximately 100% of γd,max determined by ASTM D698 or 95% of γd,max determined by ASTM D1557.

For coarse-grained soils without appreciable fines, relative density (Dr) is sometimes used for determining the level of compaction and assessing the influence of compaction on the engineering properties. Relative density is defined as:

Dr = [(emax − e) / (emax − emin)] × 100% = [(γd,field − γd,min) / (γd,max − γd,min)] × [γd,max / γd,field] × 100%   (3-5)

where: e = compacted void ratio (γd,field = corresponding dry unit weight), emax = maximum void ratio (γd,min = corresponding dry unit weight), and emin = minimum void ratio (γd,max = corresponding dry unit weight).
key_points: For soils with F < 5–15% fines, compaction behavior is less sensitive to water content and the compaction curve may be poorly defined.
Sand and gravel bulking at mid-range water content can inhibit compaction and produce a minimum γd — the opposite of fine-grained behavior.
emax (ASTM D4254) = loosest state; emin (ASTM D4253 vibratory table) = densest state; emin depends on particle shape and size.
emin from ASTM D4253 ≈ 100% of γd,max (ASTM D698) or ≈ 95% of γd,max (ASTM D1557).
Relative density Dr uses both void ratio and dry unit weight formulations and is the primary compaction metric for clean coarse-grained soils.
Particle breakage during compaction can lower emin.

equations.description: Relative density: Dr = [(emax − e)/(emax − emin)] × 100% = [(γd,field − γd,min)/(γd,max − γd,min)] × (γd,max/γd,field) × 100%, expressed in both void ratio and dry unit weight forms.

sections.applicability: Applies to coarse-grained soils with fines content less than approximately 5–15%, where relative density is the appropriate compaction metric.

sections.title: Influence of Compaction on Engineering Parameters
sections.summary: Container section covering how compaction affects the engineering properties of both coarse-grained and fine-grained soils. Organized into two subsections addressing coarse-grained soil parameters (friction angle, stiffness, hydraulic conductivity vs. Dr) and fine-grained soil parameters (strength, compressibility, hydraulic conductivity as functions of compaction state).
sections.body: Compaction produces an engineered fill with relatively high dry unit weight or low void ratio. Compaction changes the strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity of the fill, fulfilling three of the objectives in Figure 3-1.
key_points: Compaction targets high γd (low void ratio) to improve strength, reduce compressibility, and reduce hydraulic conductivity.
Effects differ significantly between coarse-grained and fine-grained soils, requiring separate treatment.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or specifying the engineering properties of compacted fills for any project type.

sections.title: Engineering Parameters of Compacted Coarse-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Describes trends in friction angle, stiffness, and hydraulic conductivity for compacted coarse-grained soils as a function of relative density (Dr). Covers the typical Dr range from loose placement (0–20%) to satisfactory compaction (75–100%), quantifies the increase in φ′ and stiffness, and explains hydraulic conductivity reduction using the Kozeny-Carman equation.
sections.body:
Coarse-grained soils, especially those with little fines, are often characterized in terms of relative density (Dr). Coarse-grained soils will have a low relative density (0 to 20%) when placed loosely. Satisfactory compaction will tend to increase Dr to the range of 75 to 100%. The trends described in this section can be used to set appropriate compaction control requirements.

The shear strength of compacted coarse-grained soils is typically quantified in terms of an effective stress friction angle (φʹ), which increases as Dr increases. As Dr increases from 0% to 100%, the friction angle increases by about 8 to 12 degrees (Hilf 1991, Duncan et al. 2014) as shown in Figure 3-4(a). This increase is also reflected in correlations between φʹ and Dr presented in Duncan et al. (2014) and Chapter 8 of DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021). The compaction water content tends to have a minor effect on the shear strength of coarse-grained soils and should usually be as high as possible.

As soil is compacted and Dr increases, coarse-grained soils become stiffer or less compressible. Based on typical values of the elastic modulus, sands and gravels become about four times stiffer when Dr is increased from 0% to 100%.

The hydraulic conductivity (ksat) of coarse-grained soils is inversely related to void ratio and will decrease as Dr increases. In Figure 3-4(b), the approximate percent decrease in ksat is estimated using the Kozeny-Carman equation. A greater reduction in ksat occurs when the soil has a wide range of possible void ratios (i.e., emax - emin is larger).
key_points: Loose placement gives Dr = 0–20%; satisfactory compaction targets Dr = 75–100%.
Friction angle φ′ increases by approximately 8–12 degrees as Dr increases from 0% to 100%.
Stiffness (elastic modulus) of sands and gravels increases approximately 4× when Dr goes from 0% to 100%.
ksat is inversely related to void ratio; decreases with increasing Dr; Kozeny-Carman equation used to estimate reduction.
Greater ksat reduction occurs in soils with a wider void ratio range (larger emax − emin).
Compaction water content has minor effect on shear strength of coarse-grained soils; should be kept as high as practical.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or evaluating compaction of coarse-grained soils (sands and gravels) where relative density governs engineering behavior.

sections.title: Engineering Parameters of Compacted Fine-Grained Soils
sections.summary: Covers the dependence of strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity of compacted clays on initial compaction state (dry vs. wet of optimum), stress history, and saturation. Introduces the 15-point method for comprehensive parameter determination, discusses brittle vs. ductile behavior, effective stress vs. total stress strength, undrained strength ratios, and ksat variation across the compaction plane.
sections.body:
The engineering parameters of compacted fine-grained soil, particularly clay, depend on the initial compaction conditions, the stress history following compaction, and the time of the design condition with respect to compaction. In particular, the effects of volume change caused by collapse or swelling must be considered. Clays which become saturated after compaction will tend to swell unless subjected to confining pressure. Swelling reduces the dry unit weight of the compacted clay and may reduce shear strength and increase compressibility. Laboratory tests used to measure the parameters of compacted clays should match field conditions to the extent possible.

As illustrated in Figure 3-3, both the water content and the compacted unit weight will affect the structure of the clay. In order to comprehensively determine the effect of compaction on fine-grained soil parameters, the 15-point method can be used as illustrated in Figure 3-5. In this method, three levels of compaction energy are selected, and five specimens are compacted at each energy, resulting in 15 combinations of compacted water content and dry unit weight. The appropriate test (shear strength, compressibility, hydraulic conductivity, etc.) is conducted on each specimen, which allows the variation in this parameter to be assessed across the compaction plane.

The 15-point method is appropriate mostly for large projects or research efforts. For smaller projects, it is often necessary to pick a particular R.C. and water content at which to perform tests to determine engineering parameters. If this approach is taken, care must be used to choose a conservative compaction state. VandenBerge et al. (2017) provide guidance on the selection of compaction conditions for shear strength tests on compacted clays.

Within practical levels of compaction, compacted clays are heavily overconsolidated. For both consolidation and axial compression, compaction dry of optimum tends to produce a more brittle response. Compaction wet of optimum tends to produce ductile soil behavior. Clays compacted dry of optimum will exhibit an apparent yield stress as shown in Figure 3-6(a). In contrast, a more gradual stress-strain behavior is observed in clays compacted wet of optimum. Under low stress levels, dry compaction will usually result in less strain or settlement. At higher stress levels, the strains tend to become similar regardless of the initial compaction state. Compression indices for compacted soil can be measured in one-dimensional consolidation tests provided the initial saturation condition in the laboratory appropriately matches the field conditions. The behavior of saturated specimens of compacted clay tested in consolidated-undrained (CU) triaxial compression is shown in Figure 3-6(b). Compaction dry of optimum will tend to create a stiffer initial response. The strength of compacted clay is about equal at high axial strain, regardless of the compaction condition. These observations apply to specimens with the same dry unit weight after consolidation.

The effective stress shear strength of compacted clay is not substantially affected by the compaction state (Johnson and Lovell 1979, VandenBerge et al. 2015). However, the pore pressure response of compacted clay varies widely by compaction state, which in turn impacts the undrained shear strength. Trends in behavior for as-compacted (UU) conditions are illustrated in Figure 3-6(c) and (d). Total stress cohesion increases with increasing compaction, while the total stress friction angle decreases with increasing water content or degree of saturation. For saturated, consolidated undrained conditions, VandenBerge et al. (2015) found that the undrained strength ratio is approximately constant up to about 70% saturation, as shown in Figure 3-7, and increases for clay compacted to higher degrees of saturation. Consolidated undrained strengths are heavily influenced by the amount of swelling that occurs during saturation.

The saturated hydraulic conductivity (ksat) of laboratory specimens of compacted clay is affected by the initial compaction state. As shown in Figure 3-8(a), ksat can vary three or four orders of magnitude within the range of typical compaction. Benson and Trast (1995) studied the hydraulic conductivity of 13 compacted clays and found an inverse relationship between ksat and initial saturation (Figure 3-8(b)). Daniel (1994) stressed the importance of field-scale considerations, such as cracking and defects, on the acting hydraulic conductivity of compacted clay liners. Tinjum et al. (1997) discusses the unsaturated properties of compacted clays.

In most cases, specimens of candidate fill materials should be compacted and tested in the laboratory to directly measure the desired engineering parameters. The trends presented in this section can help to guide the laboratory testing program. For example, clay soils will tend to have the lowest unconsolidated, undrained shear strength at high water content and low relative compaction. Thus, UU tests should be conducted at the highest water content allowed by the specification and lowest specified R.C. Similarly, ksat is highest for low initial saturation. For this reason, laboratory specimens should use the lowest specified water content to obtain a conservative measure of ksat, provided low ksat is desired.
key_points: Clay parameters depend on initial compaction state, post-compaction stress history, and saturation — swelling after compaction can reduce strength and increase compressibility.
15-point method: 3 energy levels × 5 specimens = 15 compaction states; maps parameter variation across the full compaction plane — best for large projects.
Dry of optimum: brittle response, apparent yield stress, stiffer initial compression; wet of optimum: ductile, gradual stress-strain behavior.
Effective stress shear strength is not substantially affected by compaction state; undrained strength varies due to pore pressure differences.
Total stress cohesion increases with increasing compaction; total stress friction angle decreases with increasing water content or saturation.
ksat of compacted clay varies 3–4 orders of magnitude across typical compaction range; inversely related to initial saturation.
Conservative lab testing: UU strength → test at highest w and lowest R.C.; ksat → test at lowest specified w.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining or specifying engineering parameters (strength, compressibility, hydraulic conductivity) for compacted fine-grained soils, particularly clays.

sections.title: Fill Materials
sections.summary: Covers the selection, characterization, and use of fill materials for engineered applications. Describes a six-step selection process involving sampling, classification testing, and engineering parameter determination. Addresses borrow exploration, preliminary selection by USCS classification, laboratory characterization, rock fill, and alternative fill materials including recycled and lightweight products.
sections.body: The selection of fill material for a particular engineering application must consider both the purpose and the availability of fill materials. The selection process may include the following steps: (1) gather samples of all the available and viable fill sources, (2) perform classification tests (i.e., Atterberg limits and grain-size analysis), (3) use soil classification to determine typical properties of the available fill materials based on Table 3-1, Figure 3-9, Figure 3-10, and Figure 3-11, (4) select a small number of soils to obtain larger samples, (5) perform tests to determine appropriate engineering parameters at representative compaction levels (i.e., compaction, strength, shrink/swell, hydraulic conductivity), and (6) select an appropriate soil for the application (Sowers 1979). This type of selection process may be appropriate on large projects. However, on many smaller projects, the engineer specifies the type of material, and the contractor submits particular materials for the engineer's approval, limiting this type of detailed involvement in the selection process.
key_points: Fill selection requires considering both the engineering purpose and material availability.
A six-step selection process guides large projects from sampling through final soil selection.
On smaller projects, the engineer specifies material type and the contractor submits materials for approval.
Classification tests (Atterberg limits and grain-size analysis) drive preliminary screening.
Final analysis requires testing compacted soil samples for engineering parameters.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting fill materials for any engineered application requiring fill placement.

sections.title: Borrow Exploration
sections.summary: Describes procedures for exploring borrow sources to determine quantity and quality of fill materials within economical haul distance. Specifies initial 200-foot grid spacing for mass earthwork, intermediate borings for variable conditions, and the dual purposes of establishing subsurface profiles and obtaining samples for classification, salt/gypsum content, and contamination assessment.
sections.body:
The source of the fill material is referred to as the borrow. Sufficient borings or test pits should be performed to determine the approximate quantity and quality of construction materials within an economical haul distance from the project. For mass earthwork, initial exploration should be on a 200-foot grid. If variable conditions are found during the initial exploration, intermediate borings or test pits should be completed.

One purpose of the borrow exploration is to determine a reasonably accurate subsurface profile to the anticipated depth of excavation, including the groundwater level. The approximate volume and engineering parameters should be determined for each material considered for use as fill. The other purpose of the borrow exploration is to obtain samples that can be used for classification testing as well as to ascertain the presence of salts, gypsums, or undesirable minerals, and the extent of organic or contaminated soils, if encountered.
key_points: Borrow is the source of fill material; exploration should cover all viable sources within economical haul distance.
Initial exploration for mass earthwork should be on a 200-foot grid; variable conditions require intermediate borings.
Exploration determines subsurface profile, groundwater level, and volume of usable fill.
Samples must be obtained for classification testing and assessment of salts, gypsums, organics, or contamination.
sections.applicability: Applies during project planning when investigating potential fill sources for earthwork construction.

sections.title: Preliminary Selection based on Classification
sections.summary: Guides preliminary fill selection using USCS classification and tabulated/charted typical properties including compaction characteristics, hydraulic conductivity, CBR, compressibility, and shear strength. Warns that mass compacted clay hydraulic conductivity is ~2 orders of magnitude above lab values. Notes limits on high-plasticity clays, organic soils, and maximum particle size for normal embankment construction.
sections.body:
Typical properties of compacted soils are summarized by USCS classification in Table 3-1, Figure 3-9, Figure 3-10, and Figure 3-11, which may be used for preliminary selection and analysis. For final analysis, tests should be completed on compacted soil samples to determine engineering parameters.

The ranges of hydraulic conductivity provided for clay soils in Table 3-1 correspond to laboratory compacted specimens. However, a compacted clay mass will contain cracks and discontinuities. For this reason, the mass value of k is typically about two orders of magnitude higher than the laboratory value (Daniel 1984).

Table 3-2 summarizes the relative desirability of various soil types in earth fill dams, canals, roadways, and foundations. Practically any inorganic, insoluble soil may be incorporated in an embankment when modern compaction equipment and control standards are employed. However, some soils may be difficult to use economically. For some embankment zones, fine-grained soils may have insufficient shear strength or excessive compressibility. Clays of medium to high plasticity (PI > 20 and/or LL > 40) tend to expand if placed at low water content and exposed to low confining pressures for long periods of time. Identification of soils susceptible to volume expansion is discussed in Chapter 1 of DM 7.1. High plasticity soils with high natural moisture are difficult to process for proper moisture for compaction. Stratified soils may require extensive mixing in order to produce a homogeneous fill.

For normal embankment construction, the maximum particle sizes should not exceed 3 inches (i.e., gravel-sized or smaller) or 50 percent of the compacted layer thickness. Where economic borrow sources contain larger particles, compaction trials should be performed before approval.
key_points: USCS classification supports preliminary fill selection using Table 3-1, Figure 3-9, Figure 3-10, and Figure 3-11.
Mass hydraulic conductivity of compacted clay is ~2 orders of magnitude higher than laboratory values due to field cracks.
Medium to high plasticity clays (PI > 20, LL > 40) risk expansion at low water content and low confining pressure.
Table 3-2 rates relative desirability of USCS soil groups for dams, canals, roadways, and foundations.
Maximum particle size for normal embankment fill should not exceed 3 inches or 50% of compacted layer thickness.
Compaction trials required before approving borrow sources with particles exceeding these limits.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing preliminary screening and selection of fill materials based on soil classification data.

sections.title: Laboratory Characterization of Fill Materials
sections.summary: Container section covering laboratory testing of fill materials, including reference compaction tests (Proctor and index density), engineering parameter testing by USCS group, and special considerations for rock fill including scalping/parallel gradation, shear strength nonlinearity, particle size effects, and shale durability classification systems.
key_points: Laboratory characterization encompasses compaction reference tests, engineering parameter tests, and rock fill-specific testing.
Subsections address reference Proctor testing, oversize corrections, parameter testing by USCS, and rock fill characterization.
Test methods and applicability vary by USCS classification as summarized in Table 3-3.
sections.applicability: Applies when planning a laboratory testing program for engineered fill materials of any type.

sections.title: Reference Compaction Tests
sections.summary: Describes standard and modified Proctor tests and index density methods as the basis for guiding fill placement and selecting engineering parameters. Covers the oversize particle problem in laboratory compaction testing, defines the oversize correction equations for combined water content (Eq. 3-6) and dry unit weight (Eq. 3-7), and notes that ASTM D4718 allows correction in the opposite direction (removing oversize influence from field results).
sections.body:
In order to guide both fill placement and the selection of engineering parameters for compacted fill, tests must be completed to define compaction behavior under a specified compactive effort. For soils containing appreciable fines, the standard Proctor (ASTM D698) and modified Proctor (ASTM D1557) tests are used. These tests are described in more detail in Chapter 3 of DM 7.1. The compactibility of clean soil and rock may alternatively be characterized using emin and emax (ASTM D4253 and D4254). When multiple different soils will be used as fill, a family of compaction curves should be obtained to represent the typical fill materials for the project.

Many soils contain some percentage of particles that are larger than the maximum size allowed using a given compaction mold (e.g., larger than 4.75 mm for 4-inch mold or ¾-inch for 6-inch mold). These particles are referred to as oversize and interfere with compaction of the finer soil fraction in the mold. However, in the field, these particles will be present in the field compacted fill and will influence the compacted dry unit weight.

For soils with more than 5% oversize particles, corrections can be made to the water content and dry unit weight measured on the soil without the oversize particles. These corrections are typically limited to 40% oversize for 4.75 mm particles and 30% oversize for ¾-inch particles.

The corrected water content is found as:

wT = PC·wC + PF·wF  (Eq. 3-6)

where: wT = combined water content of the finer and oversize fractions (decimal), PC = percent oversize fraction (decimal), wC = water content of the oversize fraction (decimal), PF = percent finer fraction (decimal), and wF = water content of the finer fraction (decimal).

The corrected dry unit weight is found as:

γdT = (γdF · GsC · γw) / (GsC · γw · PF + γdF · PC)  (Eq. 3-7)

where: γdT = combined dry unit weight of the finer and oversize fractions, γdF = dry unit weight of the finer fraction, GsC = specific gravity of solids of the oversize fraction, and γw = unit weight of water (62.4 pcf, 9.81 kN/m3).

In addition to correcting laboratory results for oversize as in the previous equations, ASTM D4718 allows the influence of the oversize fraction to be corrected out of the field results by solving Equations 3-6 and 3-7 for wF and γdF. An example of the two types of oversize correction is provided in Figure 3-12. The two methods do not give, exactly, the same results, and the method desired for each project should be clearly specified.
key_points: Standard Proctor (ASTM D698) and modified Proctor (ASTM D1557) are the primary reference compaction tests for fine-grained soils.
Clean soils and rock are characterized using emin and emax (ASTM D4253/D4254).
Oversize particles (>4.75 mm for 4-inch mold; >¾-inch for 6-inch mold) interfere with lab compaction and require correction.
Eq. 3-6 corrects combined water content; Eq. 3-7 corrects combined dry unit weight for oversize fractions.
Oversize corrections apply for >5% oversize, limited to 40% for 4.75 mm and 30% for ¾-inch particles.
ASTM D4718 allows removal of oversize influence from field results; the two correction directions do not give identical results and must be specified per project.

equations.description: Corrected combined water content accounting for oversize fraction: wT = PC·wC + PF·wF, where wT is the combined water content, PC is the oversize fraction (decimal), wC is the oversize water content, PF is the finer fraction (decimal), and wF is the finer fraction water content.

Corrected combined dry unit weight accounting for oversize fraction: γdT = (γdF·GsC·γw)/(GsC·γw·PF + γdF·PC), where γdT is the combined dry unit weight, γdF is the dry unit weight of the finer fraction, GsC is the specific gravity of the oversize solids, and γw is the unit weight of water.

sections.applicability: Applies when establishing reference compaction parameters for fill soils, especially those containing oversize particles exceeding mold size limits.

sections.title: Engineering Parameter Testing
sections.summary: Describes testing of engineered fill for shear strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity beyond reference compaction testing. References Table 3-3 for applicable ASTM test methods by USCS group, including Atterberg limits, grain size, Proctor, CBR, direct shear, triaxial, ring shear, hydraulic conductivity, consolidation, and swell/collapse tests.
sections.body: In addition to reference compaction tests, engineered fill materials are often tested to verify adherence to material specifications and to determine soil-specific values of shear strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity. While project conditions will dictate the specific types of information that are required, the applicable test methods for various fill materials are summarized in Table 3-3. Further description of these test methods can be found in Chapter 3 of DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021).
key_points: Engineering parameter tests verify material specifications and establish soil-specific strength, compressibility, and permeability values.
Table 3-3 maps applicable ASTM test methods to USCS classification groups.
Tests include Atterberg limits, grain size, Proctor, CBR, direct shear, triaxial (UU, CU, CD), ring shear, hydraulic conductivity, consolidation, and swell/collapse.
Designation A = applicable, M = marginally applicable, S = applicable with specialized equipment.
D3080 (direct shear) was withdrawn by ASTM in 2020 but remains an applicable method.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing a laboratory testing program to determine engineering parameters for fill materials for any project.

sections.title: Rock Fill
sections.summary: Defines rock fill (≥30% clean rock >¾-inch, <15% fines) and covers challenges of laboratory characterization due to particle size constraints. Discusses scalped vs. parallel gradation approaches for shear strength testing, nonlinearity of rock fill friction angle with stress level, particle size effects on breakage, and shale durability classification systems including FHWA, Franklin, and Wiles methods.
sections.body:
Rock fill can be defined as containing at least 30% clean rock with a grain size greater than ¾-inch and containing less than 15% fines (Breitenbach 1993). Rock fill is often placed with the major objective of creating a free-draining fill with rock-to-rock contacts throughout.

As discussed for the oversize portion of compaction test, laboratory characterization of rock fill materials is challenging because of the constraints on particle size imposed by laboratory testing equipment and standards. For example, the maximum particle size is limited to one-tenth of the specimen height for direct shear tests and one-sixth of the specimen diameter for triaxial tests. These constraints effectively limit laboratory shear strength testing to materials with particles no larger than 1 inch diameter, even for the most well-equipped commercial geotechnical laboratories. Most rock fills have a substantial fraction larger than 1 inch. Specialized large scale testing devices have been developed but are not commonly available.

The two primary alternatives for shear strength testing of rock fill with large particles are scalping and parallel gradations (Marachi et al. 1972). A scalped gradation refers to the complete removal of all particles larger than a particular grain size. The grain size distribution coefficients, Cc and Cu, of the scalped gradation will be lower than those of the parent rock fill. The scalped gradation is more poorly-graded than the rock fill. A parallel gradation is created by shifting the grain-size distribution to have 100% passing the largest allowable particle size but maintaining the shape of the distribution and the values of Cc and Cu. Creation of a parallel distribution requires a substantially larger initial soil sample and causes a more drastic change in the overall classification of the soil. Because of the level of effort and the size of the sample required, scalped gradations are typically preferred.

The shear strength of rock fill is affected by the stress level, roughness, and size of the particles as summarized in Table 3-4. Leps (1970) and others have described nonlinearity in the shear strength or friction angle of rock fill using a variety of equations. Larger particles are more likely to have defects and tend to break more easily. This effect can be considered through the parameters S or m described in Table 3-4. Marachi et al. (1972) found that increasing the particle size by a factor of four (i.e., DB/DA = 4) produced a 2 to 3.5 degrees decrease in φʹ, while the reduction in φʹ was in the range of 3 to 5 degrees for DB/DA = 12. The Frossard et al. (2012) approach predicts similar reduction in φʹ. The effect of particle size is most pronounced for rock fill with a wide range of particle strength or low m. The value of m for a rock fill can be measured using a large number of laboratory crushing tests (Marsal 1967, Lee 1992).

Two additional factors must be considered for rock fill but are difficult to quantify: (1) changes in the rock fill gradation during excavation and placement and (2) deterioration after placement (Sowers 1979). The first can be evaluated using a test embankment section and grain size analysis of samples of the fill following compaction. Potential for deterioration is especially important for shales, or sedimentary rocks composed primarily of clay and silt. These rocks have a wide range of hardness and can degrade substantially through wetting and drying, which is referred to as slaking. The most problematic shales for use as engineered fill are those which are initially hard but do not retain their properties after excavation and placement.

Where fill materials will contain shale, an appropriate system must be selected to determine the durability of the shale as well as its susceptibility to chemical degradation. Huber (1997) reviewed the available systems for classifying shale durability and recommended those proposed by FHWA (1978), Franklin (1981), and Wiles (1988). These systems use the jar slake test (Deo 1972), the slake durability test (ASTM D4644), the point load strength test (ASTM D5731), and Atterberg limits (ASTM D4318). The FHWA (1978) system divides shales into two major categories: soil-like and rock-like. The former require compaction similar to soil, while the latter are durable and can be treated as rock fill. Franklin's (1981) system provides a shale rating that has been correlated to various shale fill parameters. Wiles (1988) devised a durability rating system based on the loss of shear strength caused by wetting in triaxial tests. Susceptibility to chemical weathering is indicated by a pH less than 6 in the slake durability water as well as dark gray, green, or black color.
key_points: Rock fill is defined as ≥30% clean rock >¾-inch grain size with <15% fines.
Lab shear strength testing is limited to particles ≤1 inch; scalped gradations are preferred over parallel gradations for most projects.
Rock fill friction angle is nonlinear with effective normal stress; particle size increase raises breakage risk and reduces φʹ.
Particle size ratio DB/DA = 4 reduces φʹ by 2–3.5°; DB/DA = 12 reduces φʹ by 3–5°.
Shale durability must be assessed; FHWA (1978), Franklin (1981), and Wiles (1988) systems are recommended.
Slaking (degradation by wetting/drying) is critical for shales; pH < 6 in slake water and dark coloring indicate chemical weathering susceptibility.
Gradation changes during placement should be evaluated with a test embankment and post-compaction grain size analysis.
sections.applicability: Applies when rock fill (including shale) is being considered or used as engineered fill in embankments or other earthwork.

sections.title: Alternative Fill Materials
sections.summary: Introduces materials other than natural soil for use as fill, including recycled construction and industrial products and manufactured lightweight fills. Discusses motivations (sustainability, economics, material availability, pressure reduction) and cost factors (material, transportation, placement) as well as benefits such as accelerated construction and reduced weather sensitivity.
sections.body:
Materials other than natural soil can be used as fill. These materials include recycled products from construction or other industry as well as lightweight products manufactured for use as fill. Motivations for the use of alternative fill include concerns about sustainability, economics, lack of availability of appropriate natural materials, and efforts to reduce vertical or horizontal earth pressures.

Selection of alternative fill materials should consider multiple costs, including basic material cost, transportation cost, and placement costs. The quantity of required fill, availability of the alternative material, and local experience with construction methods also must be considered. Finally, special concerns, such as fill durability requirements, environmental concerns, and fill thermal parameters, must be addressed. Some of the intangible benefits of alternative materials may be reduced installation time leading to accelerated construction, lower weather sensitivity compared to natural soil, and reduced requirements for field quality control (FHWA 2017, Arellano 2019).
key_points: Alternative fills include recycled products and manufactured lightweight materials.
Motivations include sustainability, economics, lack of natural materials, and reducing earth pressures.
Selection must weigh material cost, transportation cost, placement cost, availability, and local construction experience.
Special concerns include fill durability, environmental impact, and thermal properties.
Intangible benefits include faster installation, lower weather sensitivity, and reduced field QC requirements.
sections.applicability: Applies when natural fill materials are unavailable, uneconomical, or inadequate for the engineering application.

sections.title: Recycled Fill Materials
sections.summary: Summarizes typical engineering properties of common recycled fill materials (recycled asphalt pavement, recycled concrete aggregate, bottom ash, fly ash, tire derived aggregate, etc.) via Table 3-5. Highlights that many recycled materials have favorable engineering properties, stresses environmental concern for leaching/runoff, and notes that local availability determines net sustainability benefit.
sections.body:
Typical properties of recycled fill materials are summarized in Table 3-5. Recycled fill materials are used as a replacement for natural soil in order to reduce disposal impacts and prevent disturbance of natural ground to obtain fill. In many cases, the recycled materials have more favorable engineering properties than natural soils.

An important environmental consideration for recycled materials is that the fill does not contaminate groundwater or surface water through leaching or runoff. It is also important to note that the use of recycled materials does not necessarily lead to a more sustainable project. For example, long transportation can offset the benefits of using a recycled material. The most beneficial recycled materials are those which are available locally, improve the engineering properties of the fill, and are environmentally benign (VandenBerge et al. 2015).
key_points: Recycled fills reduce disposal impacts and avoid disturbance of natural borrow sources.
Many recycled materials (e.g., recycled concrete aggregate φʹ ≈ 46°, recycled asphalt pavement φʹ ≈ 42°) have superior engineering properties to natural soils.
Environmental assessment for leaching and runoff is required before use.
Local availability is key: long transportation distances can negate sustainability benefits.
Fly ash classifies as ML with relatively high k variability (10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁶ cm/s); tire derived aggregate has very low unit weight (~25–30 pcf).
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating recycled industrial or construction materials as fill alternatives for earthwork projects.

sections.title: Lightweight Fill Materials
sections.summary: Covers engineered lightweight fill materials—geofoam, foamed glass aggregate, cellular concrete, tire shreds, expanded clay shale, wood chips/fiber/sawdust, and blast furnace slag—that reduce applied stresses on underlying ground. Provides unit weights, hydraulic conductivity, lateral earth pressure coefficients, and shear strength values via Table 3-6. Notes common use with ground improvement methods for soft ground.
sections.body: Engineered fill increases the stresses in the underlying ground. This can cause settlement, an increase in the stress on existing structures or walls, and a decrease in the stability of slopes. Lightweight fill materials, such as those listed in Table 3-6, can substantially reduce the stresses applied by a fill or embankment. Lightweight fill is commonly used for soft ground conditions and is often combined with ground improvement methods such as prefabricated vertical drains, deep mixing, and column-supported embankments (FHWA 2017).
key_points: Lightweight fill reduces settlement, lateral earth pressure, and slope instability on soft ground.
Geofoam (EPS/XPS) is the lightest option (0.7–3 pcf) with K = 0.1; interface properties between blocks and with soil must be analyzed.
Cellular concrete generates negligible lateral earth pressure and unit weights of 20–80 pcf.
Tire shreds/TDA (30–73 pcf, φʹ = 19–30°) can be mixed with natural soil; ASTM D6270 provides guidance.
Foamed glass aggregate and expanded clay shale provide both lightweight performance and thermal insulation.
Lightweight fill is often combined with PVDs, deep mixing, or column-supported embankments.
Wood chips exhibit 40% volume reduction on compaction; friction angle increases with particle size.
sections.applicability: Applies when fill placement over soft ground requires reduction of applied stresses, lateral pressures, or embankment weight.

sections.title: Construction of Compacted Fills
sections.summary: Overview of the compacted fill construction process, covering the sequence from drainage establishment and subgrade preparation through excavation, transport, placement, and compaction. Emphasizes the engineer's responsibility for material verification, compaction specifications, and environmental protection including runoff control.
sections.body: Compacted fills are constructed to meet some, or all, of the objectives shown in Figure 3-1 for a particular purpose. In order to create a fill that meets these objectives, the construction process starts with establishing suitable drainage and preparing the fill subgrade. The selected fill material(s) are then excavated, transported, placed, and compacted at the site. Throughout the fill construction process, the engineer has the responsibility of protecting both the project owner and the broader environment. This includes confirming that appropriate materials are used, implementing compaction specifications, and enforcing contractor procedures for the control of runoff and the protection of adjacent bodies of water (TRB 1990).
key_points: Fill construction sequence: drainage → subgrade prep → excavation → transport → placement → compaction.
Engineer is responsible for material verification, compaction specs, runoff control, and environmental protection.
Objectives of the fill guide the entire construction process as shown in Figure 3-1.
sections.applicability: Applies to all compacted fill construction projects where engineered fills must meet defined performance objectives.

sections.title: Drainage
sections.summary: Covers the critical role of drainage in fill construction quality. Discusses surface and subsurface drainage measures including slope ditches, interceptor ditches, and groundwater control. Highlights that poor drainage causes construction delays, unstable subgrades, and increased compaction difficulty, with special concern for high-plasticity clays and shale fills.
sections.body:
According to Sowers (1979), drainage is a critical, but often overlooked, component of high quality fill construction. Establishing good drainage may have a high initial cost but tends to save money over the course of most projects. In general, soil becomes weaker and more difficult to compact as its water content increases. Inadequate drainage leads to construction delays and unstable subgrade or fill soils. Where possible, surface water should be kept dispersed rather than concentrated to reduce erosion potential. As needed, surface water should be intercepted by ditches or drains and directed away from the fill area. Prior to excavation, including at borrow areas, slope ditches should be installed near the crest and at midslope to keep water out of the excavation and to keep the fill dry.
Subsurface water should also be considered by observing the site topography and knowledge of groundwater sources. The groundwater control methods described in Chapters 1 and 6 of DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021) can be used to lower groundwater below fill areas or in excavations. Surface and subsurface drainage is especially important where the embankment soils are susceptible to deterioration when exposed to water, including high plasticity clays and shale fills.
key_points: Drainage is critical but often overlooked; adequate drainage saves money over the project life.
Increasing water content weakens soil and makes compaction more difficult.
Surface water should be dispersed rather than concentrated to minimize erosion.
Slope ditches at crest and midslope should be installed before excavation to keep borrow areas dry.
Groundwater control methods per DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021) should be applied as needed.
Special drainage attention required for high-plasticity clays and shale fills susceptible to water deterioration.
sections.applicability: Applies to all fill construction sites where surface or subsurface water can affect subgrade stability or compaction quality.

sections.title: Subgrade Preparation
sections.summary: Container section covering all aspects of subgrade preparation prior to fill placement, including ground preparation, proof rolling, and methods to mitigate subgrade instability. Proper subgrade preparation is essential to achieving a stable foundation for compacted fill.
key_points: Subgrade preparation encompasses ground clearing/grubbing, proof rolling, and instability mitigation.
Proper subgrade preparation ensures a stable foundation for compacted fill lifts.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a compacted fill is to be placed on a prepared subgrade requiring evaluation and improvement.

sections.title: Ground Preparation
sections.summary: Details the ground preparation steps before fill placement: clearing (vegetation, debris, topsoil removal), grubbing (stump and root mat removal), removal of unsuitable subgrade materials, and special preparation for fills adjacent to existing slopes steeper than 3H:1V requiring benching. Also addresses transition zones between cut and fill areas.
sections.body:
After drainage has been established, the subgrade must be prepared for evaluation prior to the placement and compaction of the initial lift of fill. Clearing, which refers to removal of vegetation, trash, debris, and topsoil from the ground surface, should be completed within the bounds indicated on the plans. Topsoil is often stockpiled onsite for future use. Grubbing refers to deeper removal of stumps, heavy root mats, and buried objects. The extent of grubbing required must be specified. Deeper fills and those with less critical support requirements may not require grubbing (TRB 1990). Subsurface structures or debris that will interfere with compaction or the future construction should be removed. The sides of holes created by grubbing should be flattened, scarified, and compacted to similar unit weight as the foundation soil (USACE 1995a).
Unsuitable subgrade materials should be identified by subsurface exploration and observation after clearing and grubbing. Organically contaminated soils (Pt, OH, and OL) are generally not suitable for embankment support. Because of the detrimental effects of differential frost action, special attention should be given to removing near-surface frost susceptible soils and to limiting the availability of water to backfill.
Sites containing old fill, waste, ashes, sludge, slag, and mining spoils often require special preparation with specifics guided by the composition and past compaction of the old fill. For example, construction on poor quality existing fill will likely require ground improvement using methods described in Chapter 1. When dealing with mine waste, variable conditions can be present, including loose dumped materials as well as slurry and tailings deposits.
Special ground preparation is required for fills placed adjacent to existing slopes. If the slope is steeper than 3H:1V, the ground should be benched. Each bench consists of a horizontal cut followed by vertical step, typically not more than 4 feet high. The stair-stepped bench pattern prevents a weak zone from being created at the interface between the fill and the existing slope. In addition, slope protection in the form of riprap or drainage blankets may be needed to handle seepage from the fill or existing slope. The slope protection will help to prevent erosion and surficial slope failure (TRB 1990).
Finally, special preparation is required at the transitions between (1) cut and fill and (2) rock cut and soil cut in order to gradually accommodate the change between the differing subgrade support conditions. Material in these transition zones should be uniform without large (diameter greater than 6 inches) particles (TRB 1990). Where water may seep from the cut rock or soil, the transition fill may be used to provide drainage and prevent saturation and instability of the fill.
key_points: Clearing removes surface vegetation, debris, and topsoil; grubbing removes stumps, root mats, and buried objects.
Grubbing holes must be flattened, scarified, and compacted to match foundation soil unit weight.
Organic soils (Pt, OH, OL) are generally unsuitable for embankment support; frost-susceptible soils near the surface should be removed.
Slopes steeper than 3H:1V require benching with steps typically no more than 4 feet high to prevent weak interface zones.
Transition zones between cut and fill should use uniform material without particles larger than 6 inches in diameter.
Sites with old fill, mining waste, slag, or sludge require special preparation guided by composition and past compaction history.
sections.applicability: Applies prior to placement of the initial fill lift at any site requiring clearing, grubbing, slope benching, or transition zone preparation.

sections.title: Proof Rolling and Subgrade Stability
sections.summary: Describes proof rolling as the standard method for evaluating fill subgrade stability by systematic trafficking with a loaded dump truck or roller. Covers typical equipment requirements (30-ton gross weight, 40 psi tire pressure), the procedure for identifying deflecting zones, and subsequent scarification and compaction of the subgrade to address instability.
sections.body:
After clearing, grubbing, and other preparation, the relative stability of the fill subgrade is evaluated, often by proof rolling. Proof rolling refers to systematic trafficking of the subgrade surface by a loaded dump truck or roller. The purpose of proof rolling is to find instability and inconsistency in the subgrade or fill but not to induce widespread failure. A gross weight of 30 tons with 40 psi tire pressure is typically suitable for proof rolling of cut subgrades (TRB 1990). Once an acceptable proof rolling weight is determined, the proof roller should make two complete coverages of the subgrade and deflecting zones should be highlighted. In road construction, proof rolling can also be completed at the completion of the general earth fill and prior to placement of subbase.
The fill subgrade should be scarified and brought to optimum moisture content with special attention given to deflecting zones identified during proof rolling. The subgrade is then compacted and may be subjected to compaction control tests or further proof rolling prior to the placement of new fill.
key_points: Proof rolling uses a loaded dump truck or roller (typically 30-ton gross, 40 psi tire pressure) to identify unstable subgrade zones.
Two complete coverages of the subgrade are required; deflecting zones must be highlighted for remediation.
Proof rolling can also be performed after general earth fill completion before subbase placement in road construction.
Deflecting zones are scarified, brought to optimum moisture, recompacted, and verified before placing new fill.
sections.applicability: Applies after clearing and grubbing to evaluate stability of the fill subgrade before placing the first fill lift.

sections.title: Methods to Mitigate Subgrade Instability
sections.summary: Covers methods to address soft or unstable subgrade conditions identified by proof rolling, including bridging lifts of granular material with geogrid and geotextile, chemical stabilization using cement, fly ash, lime, or cement kiln dust, and consolidation approaches using vertical drains and preloading or ground improvement methods.
sections.body:
Where proof rolling indicates extensive instability or cannot be completed, soft subgrade conditions are present, and an initial thick stabilizing or bridging layer of sand, gravel, or crushed rock is required. Biaxial geogrid can be used below the layer to reduce the thickness of the bridging lift, and separation geotextile may be needed to prevent soft subgrade from pushing into the bridging lift. Gravity drainage should be provided to prevent water from collecting in the bridging lift. Vibrating construction equipment can exacerbate instability and should be limited until a stable working platform is achieved.
Chemical stabilization of the existing soil can also be used to improve subgrade stability. Stabilization is achieved by mixing a drying and/or cementing admixture, such as cement, fly ash, lime, or cement kiln dust, into the unstable soil. Shallow mixing can be accomplished by discing while deeper (up to 24 inches) treatment can be achieved using a specialized soil stabilizing mill. The appropriate percentage of the chemical admixture can be selected based on experience or a formal mix design that uses laboratory testing. Guidance for the selection of admixtures can be found in FHWA (2017).
Unstable soils may present concerns of long-term consolidation or low shear strength below the fill. In this case, vertical drains and/or preloading may be required to accelerate or induce consolidation (see Section 5.7.4 of DM 7.1, NAVFAC 2021) and increase the shear strength. The unstable material may also be improved using ground improvement methods described in Chapter 1.
key_points: Soft subgrades require a bridging lift of sand, gravel, or crushed rock; biaxial geogrid reduces required thickness.
Separation geotextile prevents soft subgrade from intruding into bridging lift; gravity drainage prevents water accumulation.
Vibrating equipment should be avoided until a stable working platform is established.
Chemical stabilization with cement, fly ash, lime, or cement kiln dust can treat up to 24 inches depth using a soil stabilizing mill.
Vertical drains and preloading can accelerate consolidation and increase shear strength of unstable subgrades.
sections.applicability: Applies when proof rolling reveals extensive subgrade instability or when soft subgrade conditions prevent normal proof rolling.

sections.title: Excavation, Transport, and Placement
sections.summary: Container section addressing excavation methods, borrow area management, fill transport options and haul distances, water content adjustment, and borrow/fill volume calculations including shrinkage and bulking factors. Covers equipment selection through placement and includes equations for borrow volume estimation.
key_points: Covers the full chain from borrow excavation through transport to fill placement.
Includes volume calculations accounting for bulking, shrinkage, and waste.
sections.applicability: Applies during earthwork planning and execution when fill must be excavated, transported, and placed at a project site.

sections.title: Methods
sections.summary: Describes excavation methods (hand tools, excavators, scrapers, graders, draglines, blasting), borrow area drainage and material processing, and fill transport options. Emphasizes the need to avoid mixing durable and nondurable rock fills, to manage water content during placement, and to break large soil lumps and remove deleterious materials during spreading.
sections.body:
Excavation is an important part of the process of manufacturing a quality fill and should be supervised by the engineer. Adequate drainage should be provided in the borrow area in order to maintain the appropriate water content of the fill material for efficient excavation and compaction. In addition, material processing may be required at the borrow, such as scalping oversize or mixing strata to create a homogenous fill.
Selection of appropriate and efficient excavation equipment is typically the decision of the contractor. Excavation methods can include hand tools, excavators, scrapers, graders, and draglines. In some cases, ripping and blasting may be required prior to excavation. More guidance on these can be found in Section 2-5 and FHWA (1991). Because the excavation method can affect the degree of mixing at the borrow, the engineer should be consulted. Blasting also requires consultation with the owner and engineer to determine vibration limitations, inspection requirements, and requirements for the final condition of the borrow area (TRB 1990).
Special care is required where the borrow source contains both durable rock fill and either soil or nondurable rock, such as degradable shale. Mixtures of these two materials should be avoided, because they are very difficult to adequately compact. In particular, nondurable shale should not be mixed with more durable sandstone or limestone in rock fill (FHWA 1978). Where borrow contains both, the durable rock should be separated for use as drainage fill and the outer shell of slopes, while the nondurable rock can be compacted separately as general fill.
An appropriate method must be selected to transport the fill. A variety of transport methods and economical haul distances are summarized in Table 3-7. The transportation and placement of fill can promote either segregation or mixing. If material separation is required, transportation methods should be carefully considered. As fill is dumped and spread, attention should be given to breaking large lumps of soil and removal of deleterious materials. Additional mixing of the fill can be performed at the fill location, if needed.
In many cases, the water content of the fill must be adjusted to meet the compaction specifications. Depending on the soil type as well as the method and distance of transport, this may be accomplished at the borrow area or at the fill. Coarse-grained soils with little fines often require additional water for compaction, and water trucks or hoses are used to increase the water content immediately prior to or during compaction. While water can be added and mixed into fine-grained soils, it is more common that the water content of these materials is too high. Drying can be accomplished by evaporation over time and accelerated by mixing the soil with a disk, harrow, or tiller. Chemical admixtures, such as cement, fly ash, lime, or cement kiln dust, are also drying agents and can be used when weather or time do not allow air drying.
key_points: Excavation should be engineer-supervised; borrow drainage maintains appropriate water content for efficient compaction.
Nondurable shale must not be mixed with durable sandstone or limestone rock fill; separate uses are required.
Transport method affects segregation vs. mixing; see Table 3-7 for haul distance guidance.
Coarse-grained soils typically need water added before compaction; fine-grained soils often need drying.
Chemical admixtures (cement, fly ash, lime, cement kiln dust) can serve as drying agents when air drying is impractical.
Blasting requires owner and engineer consultation for vibration limits and final borrow area condition.
sections.applicability: Applies during earthwork operations at the borrow area and during fill transport and placement at any compacted fill project.

sections.title: Borrow and Fill Quantities
sections.summary: Explains earthwork volume calculations accounting for bulking during excavation, compaction-induced unit weight changes, and waste. Presents equations for calculating total borrow volume given fill volume and waste, using dry unit weights of borrow and fill. Also addresses rock fill bulking and shrinkage factors ranging from -10% to -50%.
sections.body:
Calculation of fill volumes at the borrow site, during transportation, and after compaction is an important aspect of earthwork planning. In the borrow, the soil has an average dry unit weight (γd,B). As the soil or rock is excavated for transport, bulking will occur, which is a decrease in dry unit weight caused by an increase in the overall volume. Coarse-grained soils tend to bulk about 10% when excavated while fine-grained soils may bulk 30% to 40% (Coduto et al. 2011). Once the soil is placed and compacted, the dry unit weight of the fill (γd,F) may be either greater or less than γd,B. An average value of γd,F can be estimated using the laboratory compaction curve and assuming an average relative compaction about 2% higher than the minimum specified value (Coduto et al. 2011).
Some fill material will be lost in the earthwork process, which is referred to as waste. Waste can be intentional, such as the removal of oversize material, or unintentional. For example, a borrow with a large percentage of cobbles (diameter > 3 inches) may have a large amount of waste if the cobbles are excluded from the fill.
Comparison of total borrow and fill volumes must consider both changes in unit weight and waste. Shrinkage occurs when the earthwork process causes a reduction of volume. Bulking can occur overall if γd,F is less than γd,B and the amount of waste is low. The total weight of solids remains constant through the calculations even though the total volume changes.
If the fill volume (VF) is known and the total waste (WL) can be estimated, the total borrow volume can be calculated as:
VB = (γd,F / γd,B) × VF + WL / γd,B
where: VB = total borrow volume required, γd,F = average dry unit weight of the fill, γd,B = average dry unit weight of the borrow, and WL = total weight of waste.
In some cases, the waste must be estimated as loss percentage (XL) and the total borrow volume is:
VB = (γd,F / γd,B) × VF × (1 + XL)
The overall shrinkage factor can be defined as:
∆V / VF = (γd,F / γd,B) × (1 + XL) - 1
where: ∆V = change in total volume = VB - VF.
If more detailed unit weight information is not available, a shrinkage factor of 10% to 15% of VF can be used for estimating purposes. If required, transportation volumes can also be calculated by replacing γd,B in the preceding equations with the dry unit weight during transport (γd,trans). An example of borrow and fill calculations is provided in Figure 3-13.
Because of its dense state in situ, rock fill will experience bulking from the borrow to the fill state. Maximum bulking will tend to occur for borrow consisting of dense, hard rock with fine fracture systems that breaks into uniform sizes. In this case, the shrinkage factor may be -50% (i.e., unit volume in the borrow will produce approximately 1.5 volumes in the fill). A minimum bulking condition occurs in porous, friable rock that breaks into broadly-graded pieces with numerous spalls and fines. In this case, the shrinkage factor may be as low as -10%.
key_points: Coarse-grained soils bulk ~10% when excavated; fine-grained soils bulk 30–40%.
Average γd,F can be estimated from the lab compaction curve assuming relative compaction ~2% above the specified minimum.
Total borrow volume accounts for both unit weight ratio (γd,F/γd,B) and total waste weight or loss percentage.
Default shrinkage factor of 10–15% of VF is acceptable when detailed unit weight data is unavailable.
Rock fill bulking ranges from -10% (porous, friable rock) to -50% (dense, hard, uniformly fractured rock).
Transportation volumes can be computed by substituting γd,trans for γd,B in borrow volume equations.

equations.description: Total borrow volume required given fill volume, dry unit weights of fill and borrow, and total weight of waste: VB = (γd,F / γd,B) × VF + WL / γd,B
Total borrow volume when waste is estimated as a loss percentage XL: VB = (γd,F / γd,B) × VF × (1 + XL)
Overall shrinkage factor defined as change in total volume relative to fill volume: ΔV/VF = (γd,F / γd,B) × (1 + XL) - 1, where ΔV = VB - VF

sections.applicability: Applies during earthwork planning when estimating borrow quantities, fill volumes, and shrinkage or bulking factors for soil or rock fills.

sections.title: Compaction
