sections.summary: Container section covering all aspects of field compaction including the influence of soil type and water content on compactibility, types of compaction equipment, lift thickness guidance, and recognition of problems such as weaving/pumping and rutting. Emphasizes uniform equipment routing and controlling major compaction factors identified in Section 3-2.
sections.body: After soil is transported to the project site, it is spread and compacted in layers or lifts of relatively uniform thickness by consistent coverage of the compaction equipment. This aspect of earthwork involves control of the major factors that influence soil compaction behavior (Section 3-2), including soil type, water content, compactive effort, and type of compaction. Efforts should also be made to route equipment, such as dozers and dump trucks, uniformly across the surface of the fill. This will provide some compactive effort and will minimize the effort required from other equipment. In addition, it will reduce the potential for rutting and overloading the fill.
key_points: Fill is spread and compacted in lifts of uniform thickness with consistent equipment coverage.
Major compaction control factors: soil type, water content, compactive effort, and compaction type.
Uniform routing of all equipment across fill surface reduces rutting risk and supplements compactive effort.
sections.applicability: Applies to all compacted fill projects during the compaction phase of construction.

sections.title: Influence of Soil Type and Water Content
sections.summary: Describes how different soil types respond to compaction water content. Fine-grained soils with steep compaction curves require tight moisture control; sensitive clays lose strength upon remolding. Coarse-grained soils with less than 5–15% fines are insensitive to compaction moisture and should be placed near saturation using vibratory compaction to achieve 70–75% relative density.
sections.body:
Most soils used as fill are at least somewhat sensitive to the water content during compaction. For example, silts and some silty sands have steep compaction curves, and field moisture must be controlled within narrow limits for effective compaction. Clays are sensitive to moisture. If they are too wet, they are difficult to dry to optimum moisture, and if they are dry, it is difficult to mix the water in uniformly. An extreme example is sensitive clays, which do not respond to compaction because they lose strength upon remolding or manipulation. Soils in this category tend to compact more effectively using impact, static, and kneading compaction.
Coarse-grained soils with less than 5% to 15% fines are relatively insensitive to the compaction water content. The lower limit applies to well-graded soils while poorly-graded soils can contain more fines and still be insensitive to compaction moisture. These soils tend to have a hydraulic conductivity greater than 0.001 cm/s. These materials can be placed at the highest practical moisture content, preferably close to 100% saturation. Vibratory compaction generally is the most effective procedure. In these materials, a relative density of 70 to 75 percent can be obtained with proper compaction procedure, and relative density should be used for compaction control.
Gravel, cobbles, and boulders are also insensitive to compaction moisture. Compaction with smooth wheel vibrating rollers is the most effective procedure.
key_points: Silts and silty sands have steep compaction curves requiring tight moisture control.
Sensitive clays lose strength upon remolding and compact better with impact, static, or kneading methods.
Coarse-grained soils with <5–15% fines (k > 0.001 cm/s) are insensitive to compaction moisture.
Coarse-grained soils should be placed near 100% saturation using vibratory compaction for best results.
Target relative density of 70–75% is achievable in coarse-grained soils with proper vibratory compaction.
Gravel, cobbles, and boulders are moisture-insensitive; smooth wheel vibrating rollers are most effective.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting compaction methods and controlling moisture for different soil types during fill construction.

sections.title: Types of Equipment
sections.summary: Describes the four major compaction methods (pressure, impact, vibration, manipulation/kneading) and the equipment types that implement them, including tamping foot, rubber-tired, smooth-drum, vibratory, and grid rollers. Covers equipment selection criteria based on fill performance, walking-out behavior, lift thickness, number of passes, and recognition of weaving/pumping and rutting problems.
sections.body:
The four major methods of compaction are (1) pressure; (2) impact; (3) vibration; and (4) manipulation, kneading, or shearing. With the exception of small equipment, most compaction equipment possesses significant weight. However, the contact pressure can vary widely from high pressures under tamping foot (a.k.a., sheepsfoot) rollers to low pressures under smooth-drum rollers. While impact compaction is the primary method of laboratory compaction, it is primarily used in the field by power tampers and some operation modes of tamping and grid rollers. Vibration applies dynamic forces to soil particles that promote compaction and is used by vibratory tamping foot and smooth-drum rollers, vibratory base plate compactors, and grid compactors. Kneading compaction manipulates and shears the soil and is applied by tamping foot and rubber-tired rollers.
Table 3-8 lists commonly used compaction equipment with typical sizes and weights. In general, the compaction equipment should exert the highest contact pressure that does not result in rutting (i.e., bearing capacity failure) or failure to walk out of the fill (Sowers 1979). Walking out refers to the ability of tamping foot rollers to penetrate less and less into the fill as the fill becomes well-compacted.
The appropriate lift thickness will depend on the combination of the soil type, equipment, and fill purpose. Table 3-9 provides guidance on the applicability of different equipment to various soil conditions along with typical compacted lift thickness and number of passes. In general, the thicknesses in Table 3-9 are a satisfactory starting point. Thicker lifts may be appropriate for general purpose fills, if adequate compaction is still achieved. For water retaining fills, thinner lifts may be required to produce the desired hydraulic conductivity throughout the fill.
Selection of appropriate compaction equipment continues through the earthwork process by observation of the fill performance. When fill that is wet of optimum is compacted excessively, it deforms and deflects in an elastic manner, which is referred to as weaving or pumping. In this state, the fill is nearly saturated, and application of compactive effort is ineffective at removing further air from the fill. Further compaction can lower the dry unit weight. When the compaction equipment is too heavy for the fill or the fill is too wet, the equipment will sink into the fill causing rutting, which is a bearing capacity failure that must be fixed before earthwork can continue (TRB 1990).
key_points: Four compaction methods: pressure, impact, vibration, and manipulation/kneading/shearing.
Equipment should exert the highest contact pressure that avoids rutting or failure to walk out of the fill.
Walking out indicates tamping foot roller penetration decreasing as fill becomes well-compacted.
Table 3-8 provides equipment dimensions and weights; Table 3-9 provides lift thickness and pass guidance.
Water retaining fills may require thinner lifts to achieve target hydraulic conductivity.
Weaving/pumping indicates fill is near saturation; further compaction is ineffective and can reduce dry unit weight.
Rutting is a bearing capacity failure indicating equipment is too heavy or fill is too wet; must be remediated before continuing.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and operating compaction equipment during fill construction and when troubleshooting compaction performance problems.

sections.title: Special Construction Conditions
sections.summary: Container section addressing special compaction challenges including rock fill, retaining wall backfill, cold weather compaction, and trench backfill. Each subsection provides specific guidance on equipment, lift thickness, moisture control, and procedural requirements for these non-standard fill construction situations.
key_points: Special conditions covered: rock fill, retaining wall backfill, cold weather, and trench backfill.
Each condition requires modified procedures, equipment selection, or additional precautions beyond standard fill compaction.
sections.applicability: Applies when constructing fills under special conditions that differ from standard earthwork, including rock, retaining walls, freezing temperatures, or confined trenches.

sections.title: Rock Fill
sections.summary: Provides guidance for placing and compacting rock fill in lifts up to 3 feet thick using 10–20-ton vibratory rollers at 20–25 Hz with 4–6 passes. Addresses durability concerns for nondurable rock (especially shale), specifying that it should be treated like soil and broken down during compaction. Notes that 8-inch lift thickness with good compaction avoids major problems regardless of durability.
sections.body:
Rock fill should be placed and compacted to a dense state without large voids so that overlying material will not settle or migrate into the rock fill. Rock fill can be placed in compacted lifts up to 3 feet thick. In general, the compacted lift thickness should be at least 1.5 times the largest particle diameter (TRB 1990). Dozers can be used to crush oversized particles or rake them from the fill. Compaction should be performed with 10 to 20-ton vibratory rollers operating at about 20 to 25 Hz. Appropriate compaction is typically achieved with about four to six roller passes, while additional passes pulverize the surface without increasing compaction. The rock fill fraction smaller than ¾-inch diameter should be near its optimum moisture content for best compaction (Breitenbach 1993).
Special attention should be given to the durability of rock fill as discussed in Section 3-3.3.3. Nondurable rock should be treated similar to soil when used as fill. It should be broken down during compaction such that the large voids are filled and particle migration will be prevented if slaking occurs. This can be difficult if the shale is hard but nondurable. Problematic shales often require use of a tamping foot roller to break the particles followed by a large rubber-tired roller to compact the fill. Experience has shown that good compaction with a lift thickness of 8 inches will result in no major problems and few minor problems, regardless of the durability of the fill (FHWA 1978).
key_points: Rock fill lifts up to 3 feet thick; lift thickness must be at least 1.5 times the largest particle diameter.
Compaction requires 10–20-ton vibratory rollers at 20–25 Hz; 4–6 passes is appropriate.
Additional passes beyond 4–6 pulverize the surface without improving compaction.
Fine fraction (<3/4 inch) of rock fill should be near optimum moisture for best compaction.
Nondurable shale requires tamping foot roller to break particles, followed by rubber-tired roller for compaction.
8-inch lift thickness with good compaction avoids major problems regardless of rock fill durability (FHWA 1978).
sections.applicability: Applies when placing and compacting durable or nondurable rock fill in lifts, including shale fills requiring special treatment.

sections.title: Retaining Wall Backfill
sections.summary: Covers requirements for retaining wall backfill including preference for clean free-draining soil, prohibition on frozen material, lift thickness of 6–8 inches, and close moisture control near optimum to minimize compactive effort and lateral wall loading. Notes that material substitutions require engineer approval and references Chapter 4 for lateral pressure prediction.
sections.body:
As described in TRB (1990), lateral earth pressures on fill-type retaining walls depend heavily on the type of soil used as backfill, the placement conditions, and compaction methods. Prediction of these pressures is discussed in more detail in Chapter 4. If possible, clean, free-draining soil should be used as retaining wall backfill. Material substitutions should not be allowed for retaining wall backfill without approval of the engineer. Frozen material should not be used as backfill.
Retaining wall backfill should be spread evenly in lifts of 6 to 8 inches or less, depending on the size of the compaction equipment. The water content should be controlled closely and kept near optimum to minimize the required compactive effort and loading on the wall.
key_points: Clean, free-draining soil is preferred for retaining wall backfill; frozen material is prohibited.
Material substitutions require engineer approval.
Lift thickness should be 6–8 inches or less depending on compaction equipment size.
Water content must be kept near optimum to minimize compactive effort and lateral wall loading.
Lateral pressure prediction for fill-type retaining walls is covered in Chapter 4.
sections.applicability: Applies to backfill placement and compaction directly behind fill-type retaining walls.

sections.title: Cold Weather Considerations
sections.summary: Describes the detrimental effects of freezing temperatures on soil compaction, including increased water viscosity and higher required compactive effort for all soil types. Warns that Modified effort at 30°F produces lower dry unit weight than Standard effort at 74°F, and that ice in frozen soil will eventually thaw and soften the fill, leading to poor performance.
sections.body: Experience and research have shown that adequate compaction of moist soil is very difficult in freezing temperatures. The water in the soil has higher viscosity at low temperature. Even coarse-grained soils require much higher compactive effort when compacted near or below freezing. For example, Modified effort at 30° Fahrenheit produces a lower dry unit weight than Standard effort at 74 deg Fahrenheit (TRB 1990). In addition to difficulty compacting the soil, frozen soil may contain substantial moisture in the form of ice. When this ice eventually thaws, the fill may be softened by the additional moisture, leading to poor performance.
key_points: Adequate compaction of moist soil is very difficult at freezing temperatures for all soil types.
Modified compactive effort at 30°F yields lower dry unit weight than Standard effort at 74°F.
Frozen soil contains ice that, upon thawing, softens the fill and leads to poor long-term performance.
Higher water viscosity at low temperatures increases resistance to compaction across all soil types.
sections.applicability: Applies to fill compaction operations conducted at or near freezing temperatures (≤32°F).

sections.title: Trench Backfill
sections.summary: Introduces the requirements for compacting backfill in trenches (depth > width, width < ~15 feet), noting that even well-graded gravel requires adequate compaction and that confined access demands special small equipment. References OSHA safety considerations applicable to trench work.
sections.body: Backfill within trenches (depth greater than width and width less than about 15 feet) must be adequately compacted, even when poorly graded gravel, such as a #57 gradation, is used. Compaction in trenches can be difficult and requires special and/or small equipment. In addition, OSHA safety considerations apply as described in
key_points: Trenches defined as depth > width and width < ~15 feet; special compaction equipment is required.
Even well-graded or poorly-graded gravel (e.g., #57 gradation) in trenches must be adequately compacted.
Confined access in trenches makes compaction difficult and limits equipment options.
OSHA safety requirements apply to trench backfill operations.
sections.applicability: Applies to compaction of backfill placed within trenches where confined geometry limits equipment access.

sections.title: Control of Compacted Fills
sections.summary: Introduces the quality assurance and quality control framework for compaction control of earthfills. Explains that compaction improves engineering parameters but is costly, making the determination of adequate compaction critical. Distinguishes QA (third-party) from QC (contractor) and introduces both quantitative field testing and visual/simple measurement methods as complementary tools.
sections.body:
Compaction improves all or most of the engineering parameters of a soil or rock fill (see Figure 3-1) but is expensive both economically and environmentally. Thus, the decision whether an adequate level of compaction has been achieved is a critical step in the earthwork process (Coduto et al. 2011). This decision-making process is referred to as quality assurance (QA) when completed by an entity other than the contractor and quality control (QC) when completed by the contractor. Compaction control refers to the QA process coupled with in-depth regulation of the earthwork process appropriate to an owner's representative.

Most of this section focuses on the quantitative aspects of field testing for compaction control. However, the visual observations and simple measurements summarized in Table 3-10 are just as critical to good compaction control. Field engineers monitoring earthwork using these methods will stay active throughout the earthwork process regardless of the number of compaction control tests performed.
key_points: Compaction improves engineering parameters of soil/rock fills but is economically and environmentally costly.
QA is performed by an entity other than the contractor; QC is performed by the contractor.
Compaction control = QA + in-depth regulation of the earthwork process by the owner's representative.
Both quantitative field tests and visual/simple measurements (Table 3-10) are critical to good compaction control.
Field engineers should remain active throughout the earthwork process regardless of the number of formal compaction tests.
sections.applicability: Applies to all earthwork projects requiring compaction quality assurance and control of soil or rock fills.

sections.title: Compaction Requirements
sections.summary: Covers end-result and method specifications for compaction, including the use of relative compaction (Eq. 3-3), relative water content (Eq. 3-4), and relative density (Eq. 3-5) as control metrics. Details typical minimum R.C. values, allowable water content ranges, and lift thicknesses for various fill applications including structural support, pavements, pipe trenches, drainage blankets, and water-retaining structures.
sections.body:
The target level of compaction is typically defined using either end-result or method specifications. The number and size of QA tests performed on an earthwork project is always small with respect to the size of the fill (USBR 1987). For this reason, a well-defined compaction procedure is required for adequate compaction control, regardless of the type of specification used.

End-result specifications require that the fill be compacted to a minimum and/or average dry unit weight and may include a limitation on the compaction water content. End-result specifications may include a maximum lift thickness but allow the contractor freedom in the selection of compaction methods and equipment. Because of soil variability and the uncertainties in the construction process, the specified dry unit weight is typically stated in terms of relative compaction or relative density as compared to an applicable standard. Most often, compaction specifications use relative compaction (Equation 3-3), which is applicable to soils with appreciable fines. For these soil types, an acceptable range of relative water content (Equation 3-4) may also be specified.

Relative density (Equation 3-5) is sometimes used to determine the compaction of clean coarse-grained soils. However, Dr ranges from 0% to 100% over approximately the range of dry unit weights corresponding to R.C. of 80% to 100%. For this reason, Dr is much more sensitive to small changes in the field dry unit weight, and more variation should be expected in the compaction control tests, if Dr is used. A useful alternative for clean coarse-grained soils is to use the relative compaction concept along with ASTM D4253 as means of determining the maximum dry unit weight rather than the Proctor compaction test.

Table 3-11 summarizes typical end-result compaction specifications in terms of relative compaction for various purposes. These specifications can be modified to meet site-specific conditions and materials. USBR (1987) requirements for earth dams are summarized in Table 3-12 in terms of both relative compaction and relative density.

Simple compaction control methods for field engineers are summarized in Table 3-10. These include monitoring compaction method, compactive effort (number of passes), compacted lift thickness, soil type, soil moisture, soil response to hauling and compaction equipment, and penetration resistance. For soils with appreciable fines, visual-manual tests can assess proximity to Plastic Limit and optimum water content (typically wopt = PL - 2%±). Excessively wet soil causes rubber-tired equipment to sink up to 50% of tire width and the fill surface to weave or pump. Appropriate moisture causes rollers to track 3 to 4 inches on the first pass and progressively penetrate less deeply. Excessively dry soil causes the fill surface to become hard and dry after a few passes with little response to equipment weight.

Typical minimum relative compaction values from Table 3-11: Structural support and pavement support: 100% (D698) / 95% (D1557); Backfill surrounding structures and pipe/utility trenches: 95% (D698) / 90% (D1557); Canal or small reservoir lining: 95% (D698) / 90% (D1557); Drainage blanket or filter: 95% (D698) / 90% (D1557); Structure subgrade excavation: 100% (D698) / 95% (D1557). The relative water content range ∆w = wfield – wopt is typically specified as -2% to +2% for most applications.
key_points: End-result specifications define minimum/average dry unit weight and may limit compaction water content and maximum lift thickness.
Relative compaction (Eq. 3-3) is the most common control metric for soils with appreciable fines; relative water content (Eq. 3-4) may also be specified.
Relative density (Eq. 3-5) for clean coarse-grained soils is sensitive to small dry unit weight changes; ASTM D4253 with relative compaction is a useful alternative.
Typical minimum R.C. for structural support and pavement: 100% (ASTM D698) or 95% (ASTM D1557); for backfill and drainage: 95% (D698) / 90% (D1557).
Allowable relative water content range ∆w = wfield – wopt is typically -2% to +2% for most applications.
Lift thickness limits range from 6 inches (canal lining) to 12 inches or more (structural support, pipelines).
Table 3-10 simple field methods (visual, probe, boot heel test) are essential supplements to formal compaction testing.
Water-retaining structure compaction requirements are covered separately in Table 2-12; core material must be placed without horizontal stratification and each lift scarified before the next.

equations.description: Relative compaction — ratio of field dry unit weight to maximum dry unit weight from standard (applicable to soils with appreciable fines).
Relative water content — difference between field water content and optimum water content (∆w = wfield – wopt); used to specify acceptable compaction moisture range.
Relative density (Dr) — used to characterize compaction of clean coarse-grained soils; ranges 0–100% over the dry unit weight range corresponding to R.C. of approximately 80–100%.

sections.applicability: Applies when establishing compaction specifications and performing compaction quality control for earthfill projects involving soils with appreciable fines or clean coarse-grained soils.

sections.title: Field Test Sections
sections.summary: Describes the purpose and process of field test sections for defining compaction procedures for specific site conditions and fill materials, including both earthfill and rock fill. Covers systematic variation of compaction variables, sampling for laboratory testing, large double-ring infiltrometer testing, and the special importance of test sections for nondurable rock fills where laboratory reference values are impractical to obtain.
sections.body:
A field test section can be used to define a definite and appropriate compaction procedure for a particular combination of site conditions and fill material. In some cases, the field test section is used to develop a method specification. In other cases, a test section may be used to refine the compaction procedure. An example of the field test section process is shown in Figure 3-14. Combinations of the compaction variables, such as water content, compaction equipment, lift thickness, and equipment passes, are varied systematically. The results are typically plotted in terms of dry unit weight and number of passes.

Test sections provide an opportunity for field-scale testing of the engineering parameters of the fill material. Shelby tubes or block samples can be obtained from the compacted fill for laboratory shear strength, compressibility, or hydraulic conductivity testing. Any differences in the field compacted parameters can be used to refine the project design. Large double-ring infiltrometer tests (ASTM D3385) can be performed to evaluate the field hydraulic conductivity of compacted fine-grained soils used as seepage barriers. The results from these field tests can be used to select the appropriate compaction procedure or can be correlated to laboratory tests, which can be more easily performed.

Field test sections are particularly important for rock fills (USACE 1994b), especially those constructed with nondurable rock, such as shale. The compacted dry unit weight of rock fill is time-consuming and expensive to determine and is often impractical to regularly measure during earthwork. In addition, the engineering parameters of rock fill are difficult to measure in the laboratory without altering the grain-size distribution. A field test section allows some parameters, such as compacted hydraulic conductivity, to be measured directly. It is not feasible to determine reference unit weights or void ratios in the laboratory. The test section provides a quantitative basis for proper compaction procedures in rock fill. While gradation tests are sometimes required before and after compaction of a rock test fill to evaluate particle breakage (USACE 1994b), a field test section combined with a performance specification may eliminate the need for this testing.
key_points: Field test sections systematically vary compaction variables (water content, equipment type, lift thickness, number of passes) and plot results as dry unit weight vs. number of passes.
Shelby tube or block samples from test sections enable laboratory testing of shear strength, compressibility, and hydraulic conductivity of field-compacted material.
ASTM D3385 large double-ring infiltrometer tests can directly measure field hydraulic conductivity of fine-grained soils used as seepage barriers.
Field test sections are especially critical for rock fills (including nondurable rock like shale), where routine density measurement is impractical and lab testing alters grain-size distribution.
For rock fills, laboratory reference unit weights and void ratios are not feasible; the test section provides the quantitative basis for compaction procedure selection.
A field test section combined with a performance specification may eliminate the need for gradation tests before and after compaction to evaluate particle breakage in rock fills.
Results from field tests can be correlated to laboratory tests that are more easily performed on a routine basis.
sections.applicability: Applies when developing or refining method specifications for earthfill or rock fill compaction, particularly for nondurable rock or materials where routine field density measurement is impractical.

sections.title: Compaction Control Tests
sections.summary: Introduces compaction control tests used with end-result specifications. Field measurements of compacted dry unit weight (γd,field) and water content (wfield) are the primary outputs. Available methods are compared in Table 3-13, with emphasis on typical variability of each method and the difficulty of separating fill variability from measurement variability.
sections.body: Compaction control tests are used directly with end-result specifications. In general, a field measurement is made of the compacted dry unit weight (γd,field) and water content (wfield) of the fill. The available methods for determining these values are discussed in Chapter 2 of DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021). Some of the common methods are compared in Table 3-13, especially focusing on the typical variability of each method. In all of the studies used to collect this data, it is difficult to separate the effects of variability in the compacted fill itself from variability in the measurement of γd,field and wfield.
key_points: Compaction control tests are directly tied to end-result specifications.
Two primary field measurements are dry unit weight (γd,field) and water content (wfield).
It is difficult to separate actual fill variability from measurement method variability in reported studies.
Common methods are compared in Table 3-13, with variability as a key criterion.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever end-result compaction specifications are used and field verification of dry unit weight and water content is required.

sections.title: Control Test Methods
sections.summary: Compares common field compaction control test methods (sand cone, rubber balloon, drive cylinder, nuclear gauge, Calcium Carbide/Speedy, eGauge) in terms of accuracy, variability (SD of unit weight and water content), and time required per test. Highlights nuclear gauge speed advantages and the importance of multiple tests to reduce uncertainty. Table 3-13 provides detailed quantitative comparisons.
sections.body:
The common methods for determining field dry unit weight or relative compaction tend to have standard deviations of 1 to 2 pcf or 1% to 2%, respectively. This indicates that the range in measured γd may be as high as 5 to 10 pcf, simply due to measurement error. As noted in DM 7.1, the sand cone test is still regarded as the most accurate method, provided the sand is new, dry, and well-calibrated and the technician is experienced. However, McCook and Shanklin (2000) found that under field conditions the sand cone has similar variability as the nuclear gauge, which was attributed to the difficulty of calibrating the sand cone properly.

The time required to complete a compaction control test (summarized in Table 3-13) is an important consideration in the selection of a method. The nuclear gauge is the quickest method, being about six times faster than the sand cone. Because of its relative speed, a larger number of nuclear gauge control tests can be performed in a reasonable time period. Assuming the nuclear gauge is correctly calibrated, the use of multiple nuclear gauge tests will substantially reduce the uncertainty in the measured values of γd,field and wfield that results from either actual fill variability or the variability of the test method. Unfortunately, this perspective is not always appreciated, and the speed of the test is simply used to permit faster construction.
key_points: Typical standard deviations for field dry unit weight measurements are 1–2 pcf; for relative compaction, 1%–2%, implying a possible range of 5–10 pcf from measurement error alone.
Sand cone (ASTM D1556) is considered most accurate when properly calibrated, but field calibration difficulty reduces this advantage.
Nuclear gauge (ASTM D6938) is ~6× faster than the sand cone; direct transmission mode is more accurate than backscatter.
Speed of nuclear gauge should be used to increase test frequency and reduce uncertainty, not just accelerate construction.
Rubber balloon method may compress soft soils, yielding artificially low unit weights.
Drive cylinder tends to be less accurate than sand cone or nuclear gauge.
eGauge (ASTM D8167) is license-exempt; measures moisture with an electronic probe, less accurate than nuclear gauge but improved with soil-specific calibration.
Variability between two nuclear gauges/operators is about twice the variability for the same operator and equipment.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a field compaction control test method and evaluating the expected measurement variability for quality control purposes.

sections.title: Control Test Frequency
sections.summary: Provides minimum testing frequencies for different fill types (Table 3-14), ranging from 1 test per 2,000 CY for mass earthwork to 2–3 tests per lift for small areas. Emphasizes increased frequency at project start, in areas of doubtful quality, and at transitions. Also covers record sample requirements and the role of proof rolling for identifying suspect regions.
sections.body:
Minimum testing frequencies for different types of fill are summarized in Table 3-14. Where the earthwork operation is large and employs a consistent procedure, the testing frequency is low. In contrast, more frequent testing is required for small areas where the compaction procedure is less regular. Multiple lifts should not be placed without control testing. More frequent testing is also required at the beginning of the project as the compaction procedure is becoming established (USACE 1995a). Some agencies also require that record samples be obtained on a less frequent basis than the routine control tests. Record samples are block or other intact samples of the fill that can be used for laboratory shear strength or consolidation testing. For example, USACE (1995a) requires record samples every 30,000 to 50,000 C.Y.

Compaction control tests should be made at regions of doubtful quality, including transitions between materials, areas where rollers turn, lifts that may be too thick, lifts with improper water content, lifts compacted with insufficient roller passes or too light of rollers, fill compacted with clogged rollers, fill containing oversize rock or minor frost, and fill that is different from the average material. Such tests should be distinctly labeled as different from the routine spot tests. Proof rolling can also be used to identify doubtful regions but may be practical only for the final lift of an earthwork project or below pavements.
key_points: Minimum testing frequency ranges from 1 test/2,000 CY (mass earthwork) to 2–3 tests/lift/area (small fill areas).
Multiple lifts must not be placed without intervening control testing.
Increased testing frequency is required at project start while compaction procedures are being established.
Record samples (block/intact) for lab shear strength or consolidation testing are required every 30,000–50,000 CY per USACE (1995a).
Tests in doubtful quality regions (transitions, roller turn areas, improper water content, oversize rock, frost) must be labeled distinctly from routine spot tests.
Proof rolling can identify doubtful regions but is typically practical only for the final lift or below pavements.
sections.applicability: Applies during earthwork construction when establishing or implementing a compaction quality control testing program for any type of compacted fill.

sections.title: Control Test Comparison to Reference Values
sections.summary: Describes how field spot test results are compared to reference values of γd,max and wopt (or min/max void ratios) from laboratory compaction tests or field test sections. Covers the use of standard compaction curve families for a project, one-point field compaction tests, and Figure 3-15 showing the line-of-optimums concept for rapid field verification of relative compaction.
sections.body:
The results of field spot tests are compared to reference values of γd,max and wopt, or minimum and maximum void ratios. The reference values can come from laboratory compaction tests on the same soil or field test sections. More details on laboratory compaction testing procedures are found in Chapter 3 of DM 7.1. It is common to perform a series of these tests on the soils that are planned for use as fill, forming a set of standard compaction curves for the project. An appropriate compaction curve is selected for each lift of fill by the field engineer based on visual classification and either the relative compaction or relative density is calculated. During construction, additional laboratory compaction tests should be performed on samples of the fill, depending on the variability of materials.

Laboratory compaction tests can be supplemented by rapid, one-point compaction tests that are performed in the field. A variety of procedures have been proposed (e.g., Hilf 1991, AASHTO T272). As shown in Figure 3-15, the compaction curves for a range of soils tend to fall along a line of optimums for a particular compactive effort.

After performing a field compaction control test, the field engineer excavates soil from the field test location. The excavated soil is compacted in accordance with the appropriate test procedure (e.g., ASTM D698 or ASTM D1557), which results in a total unit weight and water content. The γt and w point is plotted on a family of typical compaction curves (e.g., Figure 3-15a). The nearest typical curve is selected, or a similarly shaped compaction curve can be interpolated. The values of γd,max and wopt are then determined from the selected curve.
key_points: Field spot test results are compared to reference values of γd,max and wopt derived from laboratory compaction tests or field test sections.
A project-specific family of standard compaction curves is built from pre-construction lab testing; the appropriate curve is selected by visual classification in the field.
One-point field compaction tests (e.g., AASHTO T272) can supplement laboratory testing for rapid verification.
Compaction curves for diverse soils tend to cluster along a line of optimums for a given compactive effort, enabling interpolation in the one-point method.
The one-point method involves compacting excavated field soil per ASTM D698 or D1557, plotting the γt–w point on a family of curves, and reading off γd,max and wopt from the nearest curve.
Additional lab compaction tests during construction are warranted when fill material variability is significant.
sections.applicability: Applies when comparing field compaction control test results to laboratory-derived reference values to determine compliance with relative compaction or relative density specifications.

sections.title: Analysis of Compaction Control Test Data
sections.summary: Describes systematic procedures for reporting, plotting, and statistically analyzing compaction control test results. Covers plotting on the compaction plane, frequency tabulations, histogram/distribution analysis, statistical interpretation of R.C. and Δw standard deviations, effects of borrow variability on reported R.C., and Hilf's two-step decision-making approach for tests outside specification limits.
sections.body:
A regular, consistent procedure should be selected to report the results of compaction control tests. At a minimum, the soil description, reference compaction curve, test location and elevation, R.C. (or Dr), and Δw should be reported along with the test results. Each test result should be evaluated with respect to the project end-result specification. Where a minimum average R.C. is specified, average values should also be calculated for the interval specified or requested by the project engineer.

In addition to the evaluation of individual test results, analysis of the entire compaction control data set will reveal general trends in compaction and may suggest the need to alter compaction methods. Two simple methods can be used by the field or project engineer: (1) plot the test results on the compaction plane with the reference compaction curve and (2) tabulate the frequency of γd and w (or R.C. and Δw). An example of how these two methods can be combined is provided in Figure 3-16. The results can be plotted in this manner either by hand or electronically.

Control tests plotted on the compaction plane should also include the S = 100% curve and the specification limits. Test points that are grouped near the edge of the limits indicate a need to adjust either the water content, the compactive effort, or both. If test results are grouped near the S = 100% curve, the fill may be overcompacted and have lower shear strength, even if the R.C. and water content meet the specification. This is of particular concern for high embankments and earth dams (Turnbull and Foster 1956). Test results that plot above the S = 100% curve are theoretically impossible and indicate uncertainty in the control testing method, error in the compaction control test, or a change in soil type and Gs value used to plot the S = 100% curve. Control tests with calculated S > 100% should not be discarded categorically but should be evaluated carefully (Schmertmann 1989).

Tables or histograms of the frequency of γd and w can be used to understand the distribution of the compacted properties. Once an adequate number of test results is available (40 or more), the mean and standard deviation of γd and w (or R.C. and Δw) can begin to be estimated from these distributions (see Chapter 7 for calculations). Simple tabulation methods provided in Davis (1953) and USBR (1998) can be used to create field histograms and cumulative distribution plots similar to those in Figure 3-16. The standard deviation can be estimated knowing that about two-thirds of the data falls within one standard deviation of the mean and 95% of the data falls within two standard deviations of the mean (for a normal distribution).

The mean and standard deviation of R.C. help to evaluate the compactive effort being used. Because a compacted fill will have variable compacted dry unit weight, the mean or average R.C. must be above the minimum specified R.C. in order for all of the fill to meet the specification. Standard deviations of R.C. for well-controlled compaction are typically less than about 3%. Higher standard deviation indicates insufficient or erratic compaction and improvement is required in the uniformity of moisture control, compaction equipment weights and pressures, or level of equipment coverage.

The mean and standard deviation of Δw help to evaluate moisture control. The mean Δw should be close to the midpoint of the specified range of water contents. A standard deviation of Δw of 1.5% or less is evidence of good moisture control. If the standard deviation of Δw is more than 3%, the moisture control is erratic, and the borrow materials may need to be better blended and moisture conditioned.

Variation in the γd,max and wopt of the borrow may also lead to apparent variation in the R.C. and Δw. For example, Hilf (1991) considers two soils with similar mean properties, a uniform aeolian soil and a more variable alluvial soil. The standard deviation of γd,max was 1.5 pcf for the aeolian soil and about 2.8 pcf for the alluvial soil. If this variation in the reference compaction curve is ignored, the reported R.C. may have a larger standard deviation than is actually present in the fill. This further emphasizes the importance of obtaining regular samples for laboratory compaction testing and checking with rapid compaction tests.

Some portion of the compaction control results will fall outside the specification limits. Hilf (1991) presents a decision-making approach for determining if such tests indicate an unacceptable compacted lift, which depends on the specification limits. An example set of compaction specifications is plotted in Figure 3-17. In Hilf's approach, the first control test is compared to the outer bounds of the specification. Tests are accepted if the γd and w are both in the specified range and rejected if both γd and w are insufficient. In regions with tests that indicate insufficient water content or γd, a retest is performed. The retest may be compared to a tighter specification because the two control tests provide a stronger statistical case for acceptance or rejection.
key_points: Report minimum required data: soil description, reference compaction curve, test location/elevation, R.C. (or Dr), and Δw for every compaction control test.
Two analysis methods: (1) plot results on the compaction plane with the S=100% curve and spec limits, and (2) tabulate/histogram frequency of γd and w (or R.C. and Δw).
Test points clustering near S=100% curve may indicate overcompaction and reduced shear strength — a critical concern for high embankments and earth dams.
Results plotting above S=100% are theoretically impossible; investigate for testing error, soil type change, or incorrect Gs — do not discard without careful evaluation.
Statistical analysis requires ≥40 tests; well-controlled compaction shows R.C. standard deviation < ~3%; Δw standard deviation ≤1.5% indicates good moisture control.
Borrow variability (e.g., σ of γd,max = 2.8 pcf for alluvial soils) can inflate apparent R.C. standard deviation — emphasizes need for regular lab compaction tests.
Hilf's two-step decision approach: compare first test to outer spec bounds; perform retest in borderline zones and compare to tighter inner bounds for acceptance/rejection.
figures: Figure 3-16 Graphical Analysis of Control Test Data
Figure 3-17 Two-Step Interpretation of Control Test Results (after Hilf 1991)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating and reporting compaction control test data for earth fills, embankments, and earth dams to assess compliance with project specifications.

sections.title: Compaction Control of Rock Fill
sections.summary: Covers the primary control methods for rock fill compaction, emphasizing field test sections and method specifications over density testing. Establishes requirements for test sections (number of passes, equipment selection) and large-scale unit weight verification tests, including minimum excavation diameter and material removal quantities per Breitenbach (1993) and Holtz et al. (2011).
sections.body: In most cases, field test sections and method specifications should be used for the primary control of rock fill (Breitenbach 1993). The test section establishes the number of passes and particular equipment required to achieve suitable compaction of the rock fill. Large-scale unit weight tests should be performed occasionally to verify the compaction procedure. Such tests require an excavation with a diameter at least four times greater than the maximum particle size and the removal of about 1000 to 2000 pounds of rock fill (Breitenbach 1993, Holtz et al. 2011).
key_points: Field test sections and method specifications are the primary control approach for rock fill compaction.
Test sections establish the required number of roller passes and equipment type for adequate compaction.
Large-scale unit weight tests should be performed periodically to verify the compaction procedure.
Verification test excavations must have a diameter at least 4× the maximum particle size.
Verification tests require removal of approximately 1,000 to 2,000 pounds of rock fill material.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying or verifying compaction of rock fill in embankment or fill construction.

sections.title: Intelligent Compaction Systems
sections.summary: Describes Intelligent Compaction (IC) systems, which continuously monitor soil properties via roller vibrations, provide automatic feedback control, and use GPS to map measurements to a GIS site model (NCHRP 2010). Covers the measurement value (MV) concept as an indicator of compaction to ~3–4 ft depth, possible MV interpretations (stiffness, modulus, vibration characteristics), and the nonlinear soil response and layer thickness effects on MV readings.
sections.body:
Intelligent compaction (IC) systems are those which continuously monitor soil properties from roller vibrations, provide automatic feedback to the roller vibration, and use GPS to map the measurements to a GIS model of the site (NCHRP 2010). The rollers record a measurement value (MV), which is an indicator of compaction to a depth of about 3 to 4 feet. Depending on the system and manufacturer, the MV may indicate soil stiffness, modulus, or roller vibration characteristics.

NCHRP (2010) summarizes the interaction between the MV and soil/subgrade conditions. The response of the soil below the roller is highly nonlinear. The MVs for thin layers are substantially affected by different stiffness of the underlying soil. Many [text continues on next page].
key_points: IC systems continuously monitor soil properties from roller vibrations and provide automatic feedback to roller vibration amplitude/frequency.
GPS integration allows measurement values (MVs) to be mapped spatially to a GIS model of the construction site.
The MV is an indicator of compaction quality to a depth of approximately 3 to 4 feet.
MV interpretation varies by manufacturer and may represent soil stiffness, modulus, or roller vibration characteristics.
Soil response beneath the roller is highly nonlinear, complicating direct interpretation of MVs.
MVs for thin compacted layers are significantly influenced by the stiffness of the underlying soil layers.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or specifying Intelligent Compaction (IC) roller systems for monitoring and controlling soil compaction during earthwork construction.

sections.title: Indirect Evaluation of Deep Fills
sections.summary: Covers methods for evaluating previously placed deep fills using subsurface exploration techniques including SPT borings, CPT soundings, geophysical surveys, and Shelby tube sampling. Also discusses the use of intelligent compaction (IC) measurement values (MVs) plotted in plan view to identify weak regions and guide compaction control testing.
sections.body:
Deep fills can be evaluated using subsurface exploration techniques as discussed in Chapter 2 of DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021). In particular, soil borings with SPT, CPT soundings, and geophysical surveys are useful to assess previously placed fills. In fill constructed from fine-grained soil, Shelby tube samples can be obtained to measure the dry unit weight of the fill. The water content of a fill can change after compaction, and correlations between MV and soil parameters, such as dry unit weight and plate load test moduli, are available.

Figure 3-18 illustrates the simplest manner in which intelligent compaction can be used to monitor compaction. The MVs are plotted in plan view to identify weak or soft regions in the fill based on low MV. Compaction control tests are performed on those regions. A more advanced approach to IC monitors the change in the MV with subsequent passes of the roller and compares this change to a specified threshold. Other methods correlate the MV to field compaction control tests or laboratory tests in order to determine threshold values of MV.
key_points: Deep fills are evaluated using subsurface exploration: SPT borings, CPT soundings, and geophysical surveys per DM 7.1 (NAVFAC 2021).
Shelby tube samples from fine-grained fill can directly measure dry unit weight.
Water content of a fill can change after compaction, affecting density-based assessments.
Intelligent compaction (IC) measurement values (MVs) are plotted in plan view to identify weak or soft regions in the fill.
Compaction control tests are targeted at low-MV regions identified by IC mapping.
Advanced IC methods track MV change with successive roller passes and compare against a specified threshold.
MVs can be correlated to field compaction control tests or laboratory tests to establish threshold values.
figures: Figure 3-18 Compaction Control Guided by Intelligent Compaction (after NCHRP 2010)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the quality and density of previously placed or deep fills using indirect subsurface investigation methods or intelligent compaction data.

sections.title: DESIGN OF EMBANKMENTS
sections.summary: Introduces the major design considerations for embankments, emphasizing that proper design and satisfactory performance depend on high-quality subsurface exploration and laboratory characterization. References DM 7.1 Chapter 2 and NCHRP (2018) for in-depth guidance. The major embankment types are illustrated in Figure 3-19 and covered in subsections.
sections.body: Proper design and satisfactory performance of embankments depend on a high-quality subsurface exploration and laboratory characterization program. Chapter 2 of DM 7.1 and NCHRP (2018) provide in depth guidance on these topics. The major types of embankments are illustrated in Figure 3-19 and are discussed in the following sections.
key_points: High-quality subsurface exploration and laboratory characterization are prerequisites for embankment design.
DM 7.1 Chapter 2 and NCHRP (2018) are primary references for exploration and characterization guidance.
Major embankment types are illustrated in Figure 3-19 and discussed in subsequent subsections.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever an embankment is being designed and the engineer needs to understand the overall framework and key references.

sections.title: Primary Design Conditions
sections.summary: Container section covering the two primary design conditions for embankments: slope stability and settlement. These conditions govern the design of all embankment types and are addressed in subsections 3-6.1.1 and 3-6.1.2.
key_points: The two primary design conditions for embankments are slope stability and settlement.
Both must be evaluated as part of any embankment design.
sections.applicability: Applies to all embankment design scenarios requiring evaluation of slope stability and settlement.

sections.title: Slope Stability
sections.summary: Covers the factors controlling embankment slope stability: shear strength of fill and foundation, groundwater conditions, and slope geometry. Notes that some soils soften over time due to weathering, climatic effects, and progressive failure. References DM 7.1 Chapter 7 for calculation procedures and Chapter 1 for shear strength parameter selection.
sections.body: The stability of embankment slopes is controlled primarily by the shear strength of the fill and supporting foundation, the groundwater conditions, and the geometry of the slope. Some soils are susceptible to softening from weathering, climatic effects, and progressive failure. Changes in the properties of these soils with time must be considered. Procedures for calculating slope stability can be found in Chapter 7 of DM 7.1. Guidance for the selection of appropriate shear strength parameters can be found in Chapter 1.
key_points: Slope stability is controlled by shear strength of fill and foundation, groundwater conditions, and slope geometry.
Some soils soften due to weathering, climate, and progressive failure — time-dependent property changes must be considered.
Slope stability calculation procedures are in DM 7.1 Chapter 7.
Shear strength parameter selection guidance is in Chapter 1.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating or designing embankment side slopes, particularly where soil softening or progressive failure is a concern.

sections.title: Settlement
sections.summary: Describes the three sources of embankment settlement: foundation consolidation, consolidation of the embankment material, and secondary compression. Quantifies expected settlements: 1–2% of fill height during excess pore pressure dissipation, 0.1–0.2% secondary compression after 3–4 years rising to 0.3–0.6% after 15–20 years. References DM 7.1 Chapter 5 and Figure 3-10 for estimation methods.
sections.body:
Settlement of an embankment is caused by foundation consolidation, consolidation of the embankment material itself, and secondary compression in the embankment after its completion. Foundation consolidation occurs as a result of the weight of the embankment fill. Chapter 5 of DM 7.1 summarizes methods to calculate foundation settlement as well as procedures to decrease foundation settlement and/or accelerate consolidation.

The compacted embankment may also experience consolidation. Significant excess pore pressures can develop during construction of fills exceeding about 80 feet in height or for lower fills of clays compacted wet of optimum. As these excess pore pressures dissipate after construction, the embankment will settle. Settlements of about 1% to 2% of the fill height are commonly experienced. Estimates based on past experience can be made using the data in Figure 3-10. For earth dams and other high fills where settlement is critical, construction pore pressures should be monitored by the methods described in Chapter 2 of DM 7.1.

Even for well-compacted embankments, secondary compression and shear strain can cause slight settlements after completion. Normally, this is only of significance in high embankments. This secondary compression typically is between 0.1% and 0.2% of the fill height after three to four years and increases to 0.3% and 0.6% after 15 to 20 years. The larger values are for clay soils.
key_points: Three sources of embankment settlement: foundation consolidation, embankment consolidation, and secondary compression.
Significant excess pore pressures can develop in fills exceeding ~80 ft or in clays compacted wet of optimum.
Post-construction settlement from pore pressure dissipation is typically 1–2% of fill height.
Secondary compression is 0.1–0.2% of fill height after 3–4 years, increasing to 0.3–0.6% after 15–20 years (higher for clays).
Figure 3-10 provides past-experience data for settlement estimates.
Construction pore pressures should be monitored for earth dams and critical high fills (DM 7.1 Chapter 2).
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating post-construction settlements for embankments, especially high fills (>80 ft) or those built with clay compacted wet of optimum.

sections.title: Embankments on Stable Foundations
sections.summary: Addresses embankment design on stable (low compressibility, strong) foundations where side slope stability controls design. Covers appropriate slope angles (1.5H:1V to 3H:1V), the influence of soil type and seepage, and special caution for high plasticity clays subject to shrink-swell, progressive failure, and fully softened conditions.
sections.body:
A stable foundation for an embankment has low compressibility and is as strong or stronger than the planned fill as shown in Figure 3-19(a). In this case, the stability of the side slopes controls the design, which will be affected by the type of soil used to build the fill and the seepage conditions. For slopes without significant seepage forces, the appropriate side slope angle varies between 1.5H:1V and 3H:1V. Steeper slopes are appropriate for compacted coarse-grained soils while flatter slopes may be required for compacted clays. The geometry of slopes and berms is also controlled by requirements for erosion control, maintenance, and mowing.

Special caution is required when constructing embankments from high plasticity clays. These soils experience the detrimental effects of shrink-swell due to weathering and moisture content changes, which leads to progressive failure and the development of fully softened conditions. Appropriate side slope design for these soils depends on selection of applicable fully softened shear strength parameters (Duncan et al. 2011, Castellanos et al. 2015).
key_points: A stable foundation has low compressibility and strength equal to or greater than the planned fill.
Side slope stability controls design; appropriate slope angles range from 1.5H:1V to 3H:1V without significant seepage.
Steeper slopes suit compacted coarse-grained soils; flatter slopes are needed for compacted clays.
High plasticity clays are susceptible to shrink-swell, progressive failure, and fully softened conditions.
Fully softened shear strength parameters must be used for high plasticity clay slope design (Duncan et al. 2011, Castellanos et al. 2015).
sections.applicability: Applies when designing embankments on foundations with low compressibility and sufficient strength, particularly where fill material type and seepage control slope geometry.

sections.title: Embankments on Weak Foundations
sections.summary: Covers design of embankments over weak foundation soils, which must address both settlement and instability through the foundation. Describes a range of mitigation approaches (Figure 3-20): slope reinforcement and flattening improve stability only; lightweight fill, load transfer, removal/replacement, and ground improvement address both stability and settlement; preloading with surcharges and vertical drains targets settlement.
sections.body:
Embankments built over weak foundations must consider settlement and instability through the foundation soil as indicated in Figure 3-19(b). Weak foundation soils may need to be partially or completely removed or densified in situ.

A range of methods for addressing embankment foundation instability is illustrated in Figure 3-20. Some approaches, such as slope reinforcement and flattening of side slopes, will only improve slope stability but will not reduce settlement. Other methods will improve both slope stability and settlement and include reducing the embankment weight using lightweight fill, transferring the load to deeper strata, removing and replacing problem materials, and implementing ground improvement. For cases where settlement is primary concern, preloading methods with surcharges and vertical drains are appropriate. Chapter 1 summarizes methods for addressing problem soils with ground improvement. More comprehensive guidance can be found in FHWA (2017).
key_points: Weak foundation embankments must address both settlement and instability through foundation soil.
Slope reinforcement and flattening improve stability only — they do not reduce settlement.
Lightweight fill, load transfer to deeper strata, removal/replacement, and ground improvement address both stability and settlement.
Preloading with surcharges and vertical drains is appropriate when settlement is the primary concern.
FHWA (2017) provides comprehensive guidance on foundation instability methods.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing embankments over weak foundation soils where settlement and foundation instability must both be mitigated.

sections.title: Reinforced Embankments
sections.summary: Covers reinforced soil slopes (RSS) using geosynthetic reinforcement placed horizontally between compacted fill layers. Explains how reinforcement improves stability and enables steeper slopes on stable foundations, and prevents instability through weak foundations. Details fill material requirements (coarse-grained, <50% fines, PI ≤ 20), installation specifications, and construction restrictions for earthwork equipment.
sections.body:
Reinforced embankments are constructed by incorporating tensile reinforcement horizontally between layers of compacted fill (Figure 3-19(c)). Most often, reinforced soil slopes (RSS) use geosynthetic reinforcement. For embankments on stable foundation, reinforcement improves stability within the embankment and allows steeper side slopes. Over a weak foundation, reinforcement can be used to prevent instability through the embankment and into the foundation soil. The reinforcement requires the RSS embankment to act as a unit and effectively reduces the bearing pressure on the weak foundation. Many column-supported embankments contain partial reinforcement in the lower lifts to help transfer load to the columns. Chapter 7 of DM 7.1 contains a summary of RSS design, and a comprehensive coverage of the topic is found in FHWA (2009). Where reinforcement is required in fill that is used as seepage barrier (i.e., earth dams), special compaction techniques are required for the layers adjacent to the reinforcement (Gregory 1993). Fiber admixtures can be used to repair shallow slope failures and reinforce slopes (Gregory 2006, Hatami et al. 2018).

Suitable performance of RSS depends on the performance of the reinforcement, which in turn is related to the selection of appropriate fill material, installation of the reinforcement, and careful earthwork practice. In general, fill for RSS should be coarse-grained (less than 50% fines), and the fines should have a PI not exceeding 20. Coarse-grained fill provides the relatively high shear strength desired for an RSS and the high level of soil-reinforcement interaction required to develop the reinforcement capacity. In order to prevent damage during earthwork, reinforcement should be installed and fill should be placed according to the manufacturer's specifications, at a minimum. These specifications will include limitations on the types of equipment that can operate on or near the reinforcement as well as appropriate lift thicknesses above the reinforcement. Construction restrictions may also prevent turning and sudden starts or stops of compaction equipment above the reinforcement. The manufacturer's specifications will also provide information about seams or overlap requirements. Special care should be taken to align the reinforcement in the proper direction because the properties are often direction dependent.
key_points: RSS uses geosynthetic reinforcement placed horizontally between compacted fill layers.
On stable foundations, reinforcement improves embankment stability and permits steeper side slopes.
Over weak foundations, reinforcement prevents instability through the embankment and foundation, reducing bearing pressure.
Fill for RSS must be coarse-grained (<50% fines) with PI ≤ 20 to ensure high shear strength and soil-reinforcement interaction.
Reinforcement must be installed per manufacturer's specifications including equipment restrictions and lift thickness requirements.
Reinforcement properties are often direction-dependent; alignment must be carefully controlled.
Special compaction techniques are required adjacent to reinforcement in seepage barriers such as earth dams.
Fiber admixtures can repair shallow slope failures and reinforce slopes.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing reinforced soil slopes (RSS) using geosynthetic reinforcement, whether on stable or weak foundations, including column-supported embankments.

sections.title: Deep and/or Valley Fills
sections.summary: Addresses settlement and differential movement in deep and valley fills resulting from foundation and embankment consolidation, secondary compression, and wetting-induced volume changes. Notes valley fills experience 0.1–2% settlement in 50 years (Duncan and Bursey 2006). Recommends higher relative compaction in lower fill zones, variable compaction water content, avoidance of expansive fill in shallow zones, and design for wetting per Brandon et al. (1990) or Noorany and Stanley (1994).
sections.body:
Relatively deep fills, as illustrated in Figure 3-19(d), experience settlement over time. Settlement can be the result of consolidation of both the foundation and the embankment fill itself. It can also be related to secondary compression over time. This behavior is especially important for dams because the long-term crest elevation is a key design consideration and for valley fills where the depth of the embankment varies greatly through the cross-section. Duncan and Bursey (2006) found that valley fills tend to experience 0.1% to 2% settlement in 50 years. Because the settlement is relative to the thickness of the embankment, valley fills may experience significant differential movement.

Over time, deep fills will experience changes in water content in response to the surrounding climate and human activity such as irrigation. In the case of earth dams, inundation will saturate some portion of the embankment. Shallow layers of compacted fill may swell while deeper layers consolidate or collapse when wetted (Brandon et al. 1990). Thus, swelling behavior can further exacerbate differential movement.

Some amount of compression and differential movement is inevitable in deep fills. Appropriate construction practice is the primary means of design to counteract these effects (Coduto et al. 2011). The lower portions of deep fills should be built with a higher specified relative compaction, which reduces the potential for further consolidation. The compaction water content may also need to be varied with lower water contents being more appropriate near the bottom of the fill. In shallower zones of deep or valley fills, expansive fill should not be used, if at all possible. In all cases, deep fills should be designed for some degree of wetting using methods such as those proposed by Brandon et al. (1990) or Noorany and Stanley (1994).
key_points: Valley fills experience 0.1–2% settlement over 50 years (Duncan and Bursey 2006) with significant differential movement due to variable fill depth.
Settlement sources include foundation and embankment consolidation and secondary compression.
Wetting from climate, irrigation, or inundation causes shallow layers to swell while deeper layers consolidate or collapse, worsening differential movement.
Lower portions of deep fills should be built to higher relative compaction to reduce consolidation potential.
Compaction water content should be varied, with lower water contents appropriate near the bottom of deep fills.
Expansive fill should be avoided in shallow zones of deep/valley fills.
All deep fills should be designed for some degree of wetting (Brandon et al. 1990 or Noorany and Stanley 1994).
sections.applicability: Applies when designing deep fills or valley fills where long-term settlement, differential movement, and wetting-induced volume changes are primary concerns.

sections.title: Earth Dam Embankments
sections.summary: Covers fill material selection and performance requirements for earth dam embankments, including zoned and homogeneous dam types. Addresses hydraulic conductivity requirements for filter/drain and core zones, internal and external erosion resistance (concentrated leak erosion, backward erosion piping, internal instability), dispersive clay identification and prohibition, and the use of Table 3-16 (erosion resistance categories) and Figure 3-21 for material evaluation.
sections.body:
USACE (2004), USBR (2012), and Chapters 6 and 7 of DM 7.1 provide guidance on the design of earth dams for stability and seepage under a variety of conditions, including end of construction, steady state seepage, rapid drawdown, and seismic loading. Earth dams may be homogeneous or zoned as illustrated in Figure 3-19(e). Considerations of shear strength and hydraulic conductivity will control both the cross-sectional geometry of an earth dam embankment as well as the parameters required of the engineered fill in each zone of the dam. This section focuses on the general properties required of fill materials used for dams. The shear strength of compacted fill should be characterized using laboratory testing on compacted specimens. The influence of compaction on shear strength of compacted soil and rock is summarized in Section 3-2.3.

With the exception of homogeneous dams, most earth dams have zones of both free-draining soil with very high hydraulic conductivity (k) and nearly impervious soil with very low k. Filter and drain zones with high k are used to intercept seepage through dams and consist of sands and gravels with little fines. These zones should be kept free of contamination with fines or the core soil during construction. Methods to estimate the hydraulic conductivity of different types of soil and to design filters between zones can be found in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1. In contrast, compacted fine-grained soils with low k are used to retain water. Compacted fill for a dam core should be free of lenses, pockets, or layers of pervious material, and successive lifts should be well bonded to each other. If a borrow source contains more than 1% oversize by mass, it should be removed prior to arrival on the earth dam embankment.

The soils selected for the zones of an earth dam must not erode under the seepage forces to which they are subjected. This includes both external erosion at the surface of the compacted fill as well as internal erosion of particles. The critical location for seepage-induced external erosion is the downstream face of a homogenous embankment. Internal erosion occurs as finer particles move into larger void spaces and can be subdivided into scour, backward erosion piping (BEP), internal migration, and internal instability (USBR and USACE 2019).

In the context of earth dams, scour refers to movement of soil particles by water flowing along an unprotected interface, most often by concentrated leak erosion (CLE). Concentrated leaks can occur through cracks or defects in fill and along unprotected discontinuities, such as conduits through the fill and foundation defects or joints. Selection of fill to resist CLE can be guided by the categories in Table 3-16. Figure 3-21(a) presents the typical gradation ranges of soils in the more resistant categories. Soils that are susceptible to CLE include gap-graded soils and soils with a well-graded flat tail, as shown Figure 3-21(b). Because CLE can occur at cracks within the fill itself, the cracking resistance of fill should be considered for earth dams. Figure 3-21(c) can be used to evaluate the likelihood of cracking.

The mechanics of BEP and internal instability are discussed in detail in Chapter 6 of DM 7.1 along with guidance on the selection of fill materials for filters. In addition, the diagonal lines shown on Figure 3-21 can be used as a preliminary assessment for internal instability. If the grain size distribution curve of a soil has sections flatter than the diagonal lines, the soil may be internally unstable. A summary of other methods for evaluating the internal instability potential of soils can be found in USBR and USACE (2019).

Dispersive clays are clay minerals that contain a high percentage of dissolved sodium in the pore water and are very susceptible to erosion. Water flowing through holes and cracks will quickly erode these clays. Dispersive clays can be identified using laboratory methods, such as the double hydrometer (ASTM D4221), the analysis of pore water extract (ASTM D4542), the pinhole test (ASTM D4647), or the crumb test (ASTM D6572). Dispersive clays should not be used as fill in dam embankments because they are very susceptible to internal erosion. Categories of dispersive tendency and associated laboratory test procedures are summarized in Table 3-17.
key_points: Earth dams may be homogeneous or zoned; shear strength and hydraulic conductivity control cross-section geometry and fill zone requirements.
Filter/drain zones require high-k sands/gravels with little fines; core zones require low-k compacted fine-grained soils free of pervious lenses.
Borrow sources with >1% oversize by mass must be screened before placement on earth dam embankments.
Internal erosion types include scour/CLE, backward erosion piping (BEP), internal migration, and internal instability.
Fill erosion resistance to CLE is categorized in Table 3-16 (Category 1 = best: CL/CH with PI > 15; Category 3 = worst: poorly compacted, gap-graded, or very uniform fine sands).
Figure 3-21 evaluates CLE susceptibility, cracking resistance, and internal instability of fill gradations.
Dispersive clays (identified by ASTM D4221, D4542, D4647, D6572) must not be used as dam fill due to extreme internal erosion susceptibility.
Dispersive tendency categories (dispersive, moderate to slightly dispersive, nondispersive) are summarized in Table 3-17.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and evaluating fill materials for earth dam embankments, particularly for erosion resistance, internal stability, and dispersivity of candidate soils.

sections.title: Side Hill Fills
sections.summary: Covers design of side hill fills constructed by compacting fill on existing slopes in hilly or mountainous terrain. Identifies causes of instability (high/fluctuating groundwater, weak colluvial or residual foundation soils) and key design measures: groundwater drainage systems, benching of natural slopes steeper than 3H:1V before fill placement, and use of conservative groundwater levels in slope stability calculations.
sections.body:
In areas with hilly or mountainous terrain, side hill fills are a commonly used method to create level space for roads and structures. As shown in Figure 3-19(f), a side hill fill is created by compacting fill on an existing slope with some of the fill material often coming from an adjacent cut. Side hill fills are often prone to instability even when the fill is appropriately compacted, leading to regular or seasonal slippage. While many of these landslides are a maintenance nuisance, some cause serious damage or loss of life. Conditions in the natural slope that typically lead to these problems include high or fluctuating groundwater and relatively weak foundation materials, such as colluvial or residual soils or degradable rock.

Although side hill fills can be problematic, they are often unavoidable, and appropriate design guidelines are required. The typical problems suggest the primary design considerations, and the side hill fill should be treated as a transition zone (TRB 1990). First, groundwater control is essential. Drainage systems should be designed to intercept groundwater seeping from the natural slope and to route surface water off the fill (see Chapter 6 of DM 7.1). The drainage should prevent both the fill and the natural soil below the fill from becoming saturated. Conservative groundwater levels, including seasonal fluctuations, should be used in slope stability calculations. Second, the interface between the compacted fill and natural slopes steeper than 3H:1V should be benched prior to compaction. Benching allows all fill to be placed horizontally. More importantly, the inclined interface between the new fill and the natural slope is removed.
key_points: Side hill fills are prone to instability even when properly compacted, due to high/fluctuating groundwater and weak foundation materials (colluvial/residual soils, degradable rock).
Side hill fills should be treated as transition zones in design (TRB 1990).
Groundwater control is the primary design measure: drainage systems must intercept seepage and route surface water off the fill.
Conservative groundwater levels including seasonal fluctuations must be used in slope stability analyses.
Natural slopes steeper than 3H:1V must be benched before fill placement to allow horizontal fill placement and eliminate inclined fill-to-slope interfaces.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing side hill fills in hilly or mountainous terrain where instability from groundwater and weak foundation materials is a concern.

sections.title: HYDRAULIC AND UNDERWATER FILLS
sections.summary: Top-level section covering the theory, placement, performance, consolidation, and control of hydraulic and underwater fills. Addresses both historical context (old dams) and modern applications such as land reclamation, dredging, and underwater construction, with guidance on soil suitability, compaction, and environmental compliance.
