key_points: Hydraulic fill uses water to excavate, transport, and place soil; primarily used today for underwater fill and land reclamation.
Placement method, soil gradation, and environmental controls are critical design considerations.
Performance, consolidation behavior, and densification methods differ significantly for coarse-grained vs. fine-grained hydraulic fills.
Underwater fill poses unique challenges related to depth, pollution control, and quality verification via in situ testing.
sections.applicability: Applies to any project involving hydraulic fill placement, underwater fill, or evaluation of existing hydraulic fill structures.

sections.title: Purpose and Use of Hydraulic Fill
sections.summary: Describes the hydraulic fill method, its historical use in dam construction, and current applications in underwater fill and land reclamation. Explains the soil-water slurry process, transport by pipe, fan deposition with segregation, and distinguishes hydraulic fill from semi-hydraulic fill (e.g., puddled clay cores, sluiced rock fill).
sections.body:
Since the advent of modern methods of excavation, transportation, and compaction in the 1930s, hydraulic fill is used mostly in particular situations, such as underwater fill and land reclamation. However, understanding the hydraulic fill process may prove helpful for interpreting the behavior of existing structures, particularly old dams, built with this method.

Hydraulic fill is a method of earthwork that uses water to excavate, transport, and place fill. Soil can be excavated hydraulically with jets, dredging, or cutter heads. The soil-water slurry is then pumped by pipe from the excavation site to the fill. Where ample water is available and large fill quantities are required, the ability to economically transport soil long distances is the main advantage of hydraulic fill. The slurry is discharged from the transport pipe as illustrated in Figure 3-22, and the soil is deposited at the hydraulic fill site, creating a fan with significant segregation and difference in the slope of the fill (Sowers 1979). Removal or placement of soil by hydraulic methods must conform to applicable water pollution control regulations. Fills that are excavated conventionally and placed using water, such as puddled clay cores or sluiced rock fill, can be classified as semi-hydraulic fill (USBR 1998).
key_points: Hydraulic fill uses water for excavation (jets, dredging, cutter heads), transport (slurry pipeline), and placement.
Main advantage is economical long-distance transport of soil where water is plentiful and large fill volumes are needed.
Slurry discharge creates a fan deposit with significant particle segregation and variable fill slopes.
Must comply with water pollution control regulations.
Semi-hydraulic fill includes conventionally excavated material placed with water, e.g., puddled clay cores or sluiced rock fill.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating the use of hydraulic fill for earthwork, or interpreting the behavior of existing hydraulic fill structures such as old dams.

sections.title: Placement of Hydraulic Fill
sections.summary: Covers methods for placing hydraulic fill on land and underwater, including pipeline discharge, clam shells, and draglines. Discusses particle segregation, achievable fill slopes (5H:1V to 40H:1V on land; as steep as 2.75H:1V underwater with gravel), use of dikes/berms for slope control, and treatment of rock voids with sluiced sand.
sections.body:
Hydraulic fill can be placed either on land or underwater. When used, hydraulic fill should be placed in a manner that produces the required usable area while minimizing environmental impact.

On land, hydraulic fills are commonly placed by pipeline but can also be created using clam shells or draglines. When hydraulic fill is discharged from a pipe, it creates a fan as the soil-water slurry spreads. The particles will segregate by size with the largest particle settling first. The fill will be wide with slopes ranging from 5H:1V to 40H:1V. Similar to underwater, dikes are required to create steeper slopes. The rate of flow can be used to control the gradation of the fill. The fine particles will remain in suspension for longer periods of time and can be removed if short sedimentation times are used (Sowers 1979).

Hydraulic fill with steeper side slopes requires the use of a mixed sand and gravel fill material or a control method during placement. Underwater slopes as steep as 3H:1V or 2.75H:1V may be achieved by careful placement of fill containing about equal amounts of sand and gravel. Berms or dikes of the coarse fill or large rock can be created around the perimeter of the fill to confine it laterally. The voids in rock placed underwater are filled with sand by sluicing to reduce compressibility and possible loss of hydraulic fill into the rock.
key_points: On land, hydraulic fill is placed by pipeline, clam shell, or dragline; pipe discharge creates a fan with particle segregation.
Natural fill slopes on land range from 5H:1V to 40H:1V; dikes are required for steeper slopes.
Flow rate controls fill gradation; short sedimentation times remove fine particles.
Underwater slopes as steep as 2.75H:1V achievable with roughly equal sand and gravel mix placed carefully.
Berms or rock dikes confine fill laterally; rock voids sluiced with sand to reduce compressibility.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or specifying hydraulic fill placement operations on land or underwater, including slope and gradation control.

sections.title: Performance of Hydraulic Fills
sections.summary: Describes performance characteristics of coarse-grained and fine-grained hydraulic fills. Covers relative density (50–60% without compaction), allowable bearing pressures (500–2000 psf), seismic liquefaction susceptibility, time for fine-grained fills to form a supporting crust (~2 years), and use of case study data (N1,60, friction angles, shear wave velocities) from an existing hydraulic fill dam.
sections.body:
Coarse-grained soils with less than 15% non-plastic fines or less than 10% plastic fines create the most satisfactory hydraulic fills. They cause the least turbidity during placement, drain faster, and are more suitable for structural support than fine-grained material. Relative densities of 50% to 60% can be obtained without compaction with a coefficient of variation of about 25%. Allowable bearing pressures are in the range of 500 to 2000 psf depending on the level of permissible settlement. Coarse-grained hydraulic fill may be variable and may contain zones of low permeability that develop high pore water pressures under seismic loading (USBR 1998). Relative density, allowable bearing pressure, and resistance to seismic liquefaction may be increased substantially by the ground improvement methods described in Chapter 1.

Hydraulic fills constructed from soft fine-grained soils, such as bottom silts and clays produced by maintenance dredging, will initially be placed at very high-water contents. Depending on measures taken to induce surface drainage, it will take approximately 2 years before a crust sufficient to support light equipment is formed and the water content of the underlying materials approaches the liquid limit. In order to allow more rapid use, a 1 to 3 feet thick layer of coarse-grained fill can be spread above the fine-grained hydraulic fill. This layer will improve the surface conditions rapidly so that they can support surcharge fills, with or without vertical drains to accelerate consolidation. Care must be exercised in applying the surcharge so that the shear strength of the soil is not exceeded.

Experience has been gained on existing hydraulic fill dams via field tests. At one dam which was constructed by discharging slurry from pipes along the sides of the dam, the resulting hydraulic fill consisted of a free-draining coarse-grained shell of gravelly silty sand with a core of silty sand and sandy non-plastic silt. The shell was generally loose to medium dense (N1,60 of 5 to 30 with mean of 17) with isolated zones of N1,60 below 5. Effective stress friction angles were determined to be in the range of 31° to 34°. The loose zones in the shell were determined to have undrained steady state shear strengths in the range of 150 to 500 psf. The hydraulic fill core was very loose to loose (N1,60 below 5 with mean of 3), and the effective stress friction angle was estimated and measured in the range of 29° to 32°. For undrained conditions, the core behaved as a normally consolidated, fine-grained soil. Shear wave velocities from seismic CPT mostly ranged from 400 ft/s to 800 ft/s and increased with depth (i.e., increased effective vertical stress). Based on these observations, new or existing hydraulic fill can be evaluated using conventional in situ testing techniques provided the engineer anticipates the spatial distribution of soil composition and relative density that results from hydraulic fill placement.
key_points: Best hydraulic fills use coarse-grained soils with <15% non-plastic fines or <10% plastic fines.
Relative densities of 50–60% achievable without compaction; allowable bearing pressures range 500–2000 psf.
Zones of low permeability in coarse-grained fills can develop high seismic pore pressures; ground improvement (Chapter 1) mitigates this.
Fine-grained hydraulic fills (dredged silts/clays) require ~2 years to form a crust sufficient for light equipment.
A 1–3 ft coarse-grained cap layer accelerates surface improvement; vertical drains can further speed consolidation.
Case study dam: shell N1,60 mean=17, core N1,60 mean=3; Vs from seismic CPT ranged 400–800 ft/s, increasing with depth.
Conventional in situ testing (SPT, CPT) is appropriate for evaluating hydraulic fill if spatial variability is anticipated.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing bearing capacity, settlement, seismic liquefaction risk, and constructibility of hydraulic fills, especially where coarse- and fine-grained materials are present.

sections.title: Consolidation of Hydraulic Fills
sections.summary: Addresses consolidation behavior of both coarse-grained and fine-grained hydraulic fills. Covers permeability thresholds (k < 0.001 cm/s indicates slow consolidation), monitoring with settlement plates, ground improvement methods (vibro-compaction, blast densification, well points), and properties of fine-grained fills including coefficient of compressibility (mv = 3×10⁻⁶ to 5×10⁻⁵ 1/psf) and pore pressure dissipation rates.
sections.body:
Coarse-grained hydraulic fills with high permeability and high coefficient of consolidation will consolidate quickly and will gain shear strength as excess pore pressures dissipate. Reasonable estimates of shear strength can be made based on estimated relative density. Hydraulic fills with k < 0.001 cm/s (fine sands and fine-grained soils) will take a long time to consolidate, and prediction of the behavior of the completed fill will be difficult. Settlement and pore pressure monitoring can be used to assess the state of consolidation of the hydraulic fill under its own weight and that of any surcharge. Settlement plates can be placed both on top of the underlying soil and within the hydraulic fill to observe settlement rates and amounts.

After self-weight consolidation, a hydraulic fill will be normally consolidated and further consolidation may be desirable. As noted by Sowers (1979), this compression can be completed by various ground improvement methods. For coarse-grained soils, vibro-compaction, pile driving, and blast densification can be used to increase relative density. Vibration at the surface of the fill can be effective to depths of about 10 feet. Silty hydraulic fills can be consolidated using well points.

The consolidation of fine-grained hydraulic fills will depend on the properties of the borrow material. Those derived from stiff clays will have a structure consisting of hard clumps in a matrix of soft clay, making laboratory tests inapplicable. Hydraulic fills derived from soft clays can be evaluated using one-dimensional consolidation tests. The coefficient of compressibility (mv) of fine-grained hydraulic fills ranges from 3×10-6 to 5×10-5 1/psf. In both cases, preloading of fine-grained hydraulic fills is effective to reduce settlements. Pore pressure dissipation rates of hydraulic fills range from hours to years depending on the sand content and cannot be estimated from laboratory tests (Whitman 1970).
key_points: Coarse-grained fills (k ≥ 0.001 cm/s) consolidate quickly; fills with k < 0.001 cm/s consolidate slowly and are difficult to predict.
Settlement plates on top of underlying soil and within the fill monitor consolidation rates and amounts.
Post-consolidation, fills are normally consolidated; further densification via vibro-compaction, pile driving, or blast densification increases relative density.
Surface vibration is effective to about 10 ft depth; well points are used for silty fills.
Fine-grained fills from stiff clays have hard clumps in soft matrix — lab tests inapplicable; soft clay fills use 1-D consolidation tests.
Coefficient of compressibility (mv) for fine-grained hydraulic fills: 3×10⁻⁶ to 5×10⁻⁵ 1/psf.
Pore pressure dissipation in hydraulic fills ranges from hours to years depending on sand content; cannot be estimated from lab tests.
sections.applicability: Applies when predicting and managing consolidation settlement and pore pressure dissipation in hydraulic fills, particularly where fine-grained or mixed soils are involved.

sections.title: Underwater Fill
sections.summary: Covers the unique challenges of placing fill underwater, typically at depths up to 100 ft. Discusses the role of dredging for subgrade preparation, primary placement methods summarized in Table 3-18, pollution control (turbidity curtains), quality control via SPT/CPT, and densification. Notes that relative density is typically 50–60% and variable, with liquefaction and settlement risks in low-density zones.
sections.body:
Some projects require fill to be placed underwater, which poses unique challenges. In most cases, experience with underwater fill placement has been limited to depths of about 100 feet or less. Pollution control, including the use of turbidity curtains, is critical during underwater fill construction.

Dredging is an important part of the underwater fill placement process similar to subgrade preparation for conventional fill. Dredging can be used to remove unsuitable soil, cut slopes in existing submerged materials, and clean the fill area. At a minimum, the latter is required to remove settled fine-grained material resulting from the construction activity (Johnson et al. 1972).

The primary methods of placing fill underwater are summarized in Table 3-18. The placement method will be governed by the available equipment, the depth of water, and the required side slopes. Fill quantities are tracked by bathymetric methods. The effects of settlement during construction on the measured fill quantities should be considered.

Control of underwater fill is typically completed using in situ testing techniques, such as SPT or CPT. Testing should be completed as placement of the fill progresses, particularly to check for unsuitable materials trapped below or within the fill. Samplers can be used, if necessary, to obtain physical samples of the underwater fill. Experience has shown that large, rugged sampling techniques are more effective than refined, sophisticated ones (Bazett and Foxall 1972).

The relative density of underwater fill is typically up to 50% to 60% and is highly variable. Zones of low relative density may be a concern for settlement under moderate to heavy loads and for liquefaction. Vibro-compaction is the primary method used to densify hydraulic and underwater fills after placement. Examples include dry docks (Zola and Boothe 1960), dams (Hassouna and Shenouda 1970), and man-made islands.
key_points: Underwater fill experience is largely limited to depths of 100 ft or less; pollution control (turbidity curtains) is critical.
Dredging is required for subgrade preparation: removes unsuitable soil, cuts slopes, and clears settled fines.
Placement method depends on equipment, water depth, and required side slopes; fill quantities tracked by bathymetric methods.
Quality control uses SPT or CPT conducted progressively during fill placement; rugged sampling techniques preferred.
Underwater fill relative density is typically 50–60% and highly variable; low-density zones risk settlement and liquefaction.
Vibro-compaction is the primary post-placement densification method for hydraulic and underwater fills.
sections.applicability: Applies to projects requiring fill placement in submerged conditions, including dry docks, dams, and man-made islands, at depths generally up to 100 ft.

sections.title: PROBLEM SOILS AND EARTHWORK
sections.summary: Introduces problem soil conditions relevant to earthwork design, referencing Chapter 1 for a broader summary of soil types and directing the reader to Table 3-19, which consolidates primary earthwork design considerations for each problematic soil category including soft clays, expansive clays, collapsible soils, loose sands, organic soils, dispersive soils, and others.
sections.body: Chapter 1 provides a summary of many types of problem soil conditions that can affect the design of foundations and earth structures. Table 3-19 summarizes important conditions for the design of earthwork in problem soils.
key_points: Chapter 1 provides a broader taxonomy of problem soil types affecting foundations and earth structures.
Table 3-19 is the primary reference for earthwork design considerations specific to each problematic soil category.
Soft clays and organic soils require mechanical or chemical stabilization and/or staged construction before fill compaction can proceed.
Highly plastic expansive clays and shales require slope design based on fully-softened shear strength parameters due to shrink-swell behavior.
Collapsible soils (e.g., loess) risk compression under earthwork loading, especially when combined with moisture changes; compacting wet of optimum reduces risk.
Sensitive clays require a high factor of safety ensuring shear stresses remain below peak shear strength at all points.
Dispersive soils are susceptible to internal erosion and should be avoided in seepage barriers such as earth dams or levees.
In seismic zones, loose sands beneath or within embankments present a liquefaction hazard that must be evaluated.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing earthwork (fills, embankments, subgrades) over or using any of the listed problem soil types.

Earth dam construction is covered by USACE EM 1110-2-2300 (2004) and USBR Design Standards No. 13, Chapter 10 (2012).
Rock fill placement and compaction guidelines are addressed in Breitenbach (1993) in the Geotechnical Testing Journal.
Underwater fill construction and testing is referenced via ASTM Special Technical Publication 501.
References span government agency manuals (USACE, USBR), national research council reports (TRB), and peer-reviewed journal articles.
sections.applicability: Applies when engineers seek additional technical guidance beyond Chapter 3 on earthwork, compacted fill, earth and rock-fill dams, rockfill, or underwater fill construction.
